stories.body:
Barbara Kingsolver’s new book is a canny feat of art imitating art. Partita is about a pianist, Livia, looking back at her life and trying to understand what art means to her.

It’s structured the same way the composition from which it takes its name is. A partita consists of a series of dance movements, typically written for a solo instrument, that vary in pace and mood. All these parts must come together to form the whole. In much the same way, Livia and the reader must bring these movements together to achieve a sense of completeness and understanding.

Each chapter is named for the various elements common in musical compositions and they follow their moods and pace. For instance, the novel’s sarabande chapter is calm, reflective, or emotionally intense like it would be in a piece of music. In this way, the book doesn’t have a linear structure as various chapters serve as refrains (a rondo) or go back to the beginning (Da Capo).

The story alternates between formative events from Livia’s adolescence and early adulthood as well as the present when Livia is in her mid-40s. As the pieces come together, we see Livia as a whole. She was a prodigious young piano talent working hard to keep up her prestigious scholarship. She then gets pulled into the exciting world of an older trade unionist and starts questioning everything. In the present, she has become a middle-aged woman who is an inspirational local music teacher in Tennessee.

Our reviewer found Partita to be a virtuosic work that in its inventiveness creates a fascinating character study of a middle-aged woman’s life and relationships. This book is a testament to the importance of access to art and celebrates those who help provide it. In this vein, I really enjoyed the listening list of classical songs that Kingsolver provides to accompany your reading. This in itself is a quiet but lovely gesture, as our reviewer notes, “including [the reader] in a world that may feel out of reach”.

Partita by Barbara Kingsolver is out now

Read more: Partita by Barbara Kingsolver: the touching story of a musician striving to bring the movements of her life together

Painters of different persuasions

Another American who wanted us to questions our relationship to and how we consume art was Robert Ryman.

Ryman thought that “you cannot understand a painting by explaining something. You can only understand painting by experience”. And so, in his show, Robert Ryman: The Real Thing, at London’s Barbican you won’t find much information to go on. In fact, as our reviewer can attest to, there arnen’t even labels to identify the paintings.

Bringing together 68 works from the mid-1950s to the early 2010s, this is a show that demands your attention. There are a lot of white canvases, which if you glance over seem indistinguishable but you need to look closer. Every choice the curators have made – from the lack of information to the way the lighting is directed – forces the viewer to engage. This is a difficult show in a modern age where our brains refuse to sit still and I think it is a challenge many of us should take on.

Robert Ryman: The Real Thing is on at Barbican Art Gallery, London until February 28 2027

Read more: Robert Ryman: The Real Thing at the Barbican – these mesmerising paintings must be seen in person

If you’re looking for something a bit more traditional then you can catch Renoir and Love at The National Portrait Gallery. Now the title would make you think you might be confronted with rooms full of his kistch nudes, however, this show is more a celebration of life’s many loves – from a good catch up with friends and a dance to that wonderful feeling you get after a very good meal.

It is an ambitious show bringing together his breakthrough impressionist paintings from the 1860s to 1880s. Our reviewer was in awe of Dance at the Moulin de la Galette (1876) in particular. Getting to see this impressive, large painting, he described the experience of seeing it in the flesh as startling.

Renoir and Love is on at The National Gallery, London until January 31 2027

Read more: Renoir and Love is a wonderful celebration of the fleeting joys of life

Uncovering the truth

On the big screen this week comes the follow-up to The Social Network. The Social Reckoning shows a company and a CEO which have become very different beasts. There’s been a mutation of Mark Zuckerberg from awkward nerd (played by Jessie Eisenberg) to sinister billionaire CEO of tech conglomerate Meta (played now by Sucession’s Jeremy Strong). Meta is also now a company that in Zuckberg’s words sees itself as “post-government” and is doing untold damage to the world through social media.

The Social Reckoning is part of the growing genre of films about crusading journalists trying to break a big corruption story. Think Spotlight (2015) about Boston Globe journalists who uncover systemic cover-ups of sexual abuse within the Catholic Church. Here, we follow The Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz and engineer Frances Haugen whose conscience drives her to whistleblow on some of the company’s most guarded secrets. Our reviewer thought it was remarkable, especially in how it reflects a world increasingly managed by Silicon Valley logic.

The Social Reckoning is in cinemas now

On the small screen, we’re into the second week of Celebrity Traitors and boy are things already juicy. What was Richard E Grant thinking? If you’ve not caught up yet, that is all I will say.

In this piece, psychology scholar Paddy Ross explains what effect fame has on the game. What impact does being a fan of model Jerry Hall have on how trustworthy you think she is or how much you like the work of comedian Romesh Ranganathan? From the “big dog” theory to halo and the horn effect, Ross outlines who might benefit from being known.

stories.body:
On 9 October 1876, Solomon Tshekisho “Sol” Plaatje was born in the rural interior of what is now South Africa. He was raised in a Setswana -speaking Barolong family and grew up on a German mission station in the then Cape Colony.

At this time, the region was made up of a mix of British colonies, independent Boer republics, and territories under African control. It was only in 1910 that white rule would be consolidated under the nation state of South Africa. Race policies hardened, ultimately developing into the adoption of apartheid in 1948.

Read more: Anniversaries spark renewed readings of South Africa’s celebrated Sol Plaatje

By the time of his death in 1932, Plaatje was one of the most respected and prominent Black people of his generation, recognised for his abilities even by his detractors. Today Plaatje may be best known as a pioneering journalist, newspaper editor and writer, a campaigner for rights, and founding general secretary of the resistance movement that would one day govern a democratic South Africa, the African National Congress . But he was much more besides, as research continues to reveal.

As a scholar of South African literary and intellectual traditions, I have researched Plaatje and his work for many years. In my view, he matters today on the world stage and across so many realms because his legacy has both influenced and transcended politics in South Africa. It connects to wider movements and efforts for meaningful change and innovation.

He refused to let his fight against racial injustice and subjugation remain isolated. He understood that the British Empire operated worldwide, and actively connected with key figures in the global Black diaspora on his travels and through correspondence. He also formed ties with the women’s suffrage movement. He spoke out in support of African migrant workers in South Africa. He interacted with universities at home and abroad, which opened up new understandings of Africa.

Plaatje’s legacy is compelling also in that it merged insights and elements from across knowledge systems, languages and creative practices, which he put in conversation with each other. His friends called him the “ walking library ” because of his grasp of literatures from far and wide, as well as oral histories, news and commentaries. His reading included Shakespeare, whose plays he would go on to translate . He drew on this rich mix to engage with prime ministers, leaders of different persuasions, crowds in a range of countries, readers of diverse publications, and ordinary people he met on his way.

Plaatje himself kept looking back in order to speak to the present and future. In his 1916 protest book, Native Life in South Africa , for example, he elaborated on times past to highlight “changes for the worse” instigated by the then new 1913 Natives Land Act . In his 1930 novel Mhudi , he zeroed in on the era of the Great Trek a century earlier, involving a temporary alliance between the Barolong and Boers. It offered a kind of corrective to official Afrikaner versions, while also widening Barolong historiography about the conflict with the Matabele.

His 150th birthday propels us to do the same: to make considered assessments of what has gone before so we can recalibrate our outlook and renew efforts for change.

New insights

In recent years, we have seen major new South African biographical treatments of Plaatje offer deeper dives into a life lived to the full and pushed to the extreme.

These have come in the form of historian Brian Willan’s expansive Sol T. Plaatje: A Life (2018) and writer Sabata-Mpho Mokae’s evocative translation into Setswana of the late doctor and teacher Modiri Molema’s 1965 manuscript in English, Solomon Tshekisho Plaatje: Lover of His People (2022).

The biographical approach has been complemented by historian Khumisho Moguerane’s Morafe: Person, Family and Nation in Colonial Bechuanaland, 1880s-1950 . This kind of work has implications for how we think about Plaatje – not only as a stand-out national figure in his own right, but embedded in community tied together by civic and moral values.

Sol T. Plaatje: A Life in Letters (2020) adds further to our understanding of Plaatje’s inner life and versatility. It includes many letters in Setswana and in translation. Later letters shed light on his shift from frontline political activism toward radical language preservation of Setswana. He saw these efforts as inextricably intertwined.

African languages

Adding to this important emphasis on language are recent re-evaluations of Plaatje’s works. One is Mhudi , considered the first full-length novel in English to have been written by a black South African. Another is his earlier Mafeking Diary , written while under siege in the South African War .

One aspect centres on the tensions and possibilities of writing across languages and cultures: English, the language introduced by imperial Britain, and Setswana with its deep underpinnings of spoken or oral culture.

Out, too, in time for the 150th anniversary, is a new edition of Sol Plaatje: Selected Writings . It collates key contributions by Plaatje in English, illustrating how he influenced early debates on land, citizenship, translation, and many other issues. Editor Brian Willan points, too, to the work of academics like Mokae and Lesley Mofokeng in illuminating Plaatje’s writing in Setswana, furthering the decolonising project.

Scholar Bhekizizwe Peterson underlined how Plaatje advocated for African languages to take up their rightful place in an appreciation of “world culture”.

Then and now, African languages remain largely under-acknowledged. Their promotion and preservation lack support compared with those considered to be at the global “centre”. To add to the complexity, in an age of artificial intelligence (AI), African languages occupy a notably under-represented position in global AI systems, increasing the risk of Africa’s greater marginalisation.

Studying, nurturing, and giving due credence to African languages played no small part in Plaatje’s life work. And yet it was no contradiction that he excelled in English and other “imposed” languages.

There is a long way to go in securing the prominence of African languages. But there are also impressive Africa-based technology initiatives working to achieve meaningful participation for African languages in the AI knowledge domain, while protecting the continent’s cultural capital, languages and data sovereignty. To do this is to take up Plaatje’s call in the new era.

stories.title: Ken Paxton’s Security for Travel Cost Taxpayers Millions. Just 1 in 6 of His Trips Had a Stated Business Purpose.
stories.summary: The post Ken Paxton’s Security for Travel Cost Taxpayers Millions. Just 1 in 6 of His Trips Had a Stated Business Purpose. appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.imageAlt: A document showing a Texas Department of Public Safety expense report listing out-of-state and in-state executive protection travel costs for the attorney general in the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2023.
stories.body:
Records show the Texas attorney general has taken nearly 1,000 trips during his tenure, costing $3.3 million in security. We could only connect 138 of those trips and $553,000 in security costs to state business.

Co-published with The Texas Tribune

In the summer of 2023, after he was impeached on charges of abusing his office for personal gain, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton was suspended and barred from conducting any official business for more than three months while awaiting trial in the state Senate.

So, he traveled.

Paxton, a Republican who is now running for U.S. Senate, took at least 17 trips over three months, including to resort destinations Park City, Utah, and Vail, Colorado. He visited the Oklahoma town where he owns a vacation lodge and a Utah community with a golf resort, where he later bought four condominiums.

State police joined him each time, costing taxpayers tens of thousands of dollars for trips unrelated to his job as attorney general. The Texas Senate ultimately acquitted him on the impeachment charges.

But Paxton’s use of the taxpayer-funded detail did not begin or end there. In fact, it stands out compared with his predecessor, fellow elected officials in Texas and other state attorneys general, ProPublica and The Texas Tribune found.

Paxton has traveled frequently out of state while listing little on his official calendar, The Associated Press reported last week . ProPublica and the Tribune’s analysis, which included reviewing every publicly available document Paxton’s office says it possesses about his travel, discloses for the first time how few of his trips had a listed business purpose: just 1 in 6.

It also found Paxton’s security has cost taxpayers far more than has previously been reported.

Since assuming office in 2015, Paxton has taken nearly 1,000 trips with a state-funded security detail, costing $3.3 million. The newsrooms’ review of Paxton’s travel records, obtained through the state’s Public Information Act, could only connect 138 of those trips and $553,000 in security costs to state business.

Records detailing the purpose of Paxton’s visits to 36 states and 19 countries do not appear to exist in most cases. These include a trip to a small town in Hawaii months before his family’s blind trust bought land there; 24 trips to Utah, where the trust owns five properties; and 53 trips to Florida, where Paxton and the trust have two houses and a townhome.

“If you’ve got all these extra trips, it becomes ethically and morally problematic,” said Chris Toth, former executive director of the National Association of Attorneys General, who has also criticized Paxton’s conduct on other issues. “The ethical question is whether a legitimate security function has effectively become a taxpayer-funded subsidy.”

Texas law allows the Department of Public Safety to provide security for key state leaders, including the attorney general, but does not require officials to use it. In fact, Paxton himself hasn’t used it in at least two dozen cases while traveling on official business.

Paxton has dismissed opponents’ attacks that he has used the perks of office to benefit himself and has not answered questions about how he vastly increased his wealth as a public servant.

He also did not answer detailed questions for this story. ProPublica and the Tribune sent Paxton a spreadsheet detailing travel for which there was no record that he was on state business and asked him to provide additional information if the trips were not personal. Neither Paxton nor his office provided such records. Instead, his office provided a general statement.

“Throughout his career, Ken Paxton has faced numerous security threats stemming from his courageous work as Attorney General fighting on behalf of the people of Texas,” his office said in the statement. “Those threats are a direct result of him taking on the cartels terrorizing Texans and some of the nation’s most dangerous violent criminals.”

Paxton’s office directed additional questions to DPS.

A DPS spokesperson declined to answer the newsrooms’ questions, saying the agency does not comment on its security arrangements.

An Outlier Among Peers

To analyze Paxton’s travel, ProPublica and the Tribune reviewed DPS logs for his security detail and records from the attorney general’s office, including airfare and lodging receipts, per diems and his daily calendars.

The records available for his predecessor, Greg Abbott , show a stark difference: Abbott traveled mostly within the state as attorney general, and his security cost $203,000 during his last three years in the office. Adjusted for inflation, Abbott’s security detail cost $7,400 per month. Paxton’s has averaged $24,300.

Because the state keeps records only for a limited time, Abbott’s travel expenses and his daily calendars as attorney general no longer exist, so the news organizations could not determine how many of his trips were for business.

Records are available, however, for Abbott’s security costs as governor and for Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick . Both are also offered state police security and have been in their current roles as long as Paxton.

When compared, the records show Paxton has taken 82 more out-of-state trips with a security detail than Abbott and nearly as many as the governor and lieutenant governor combined.

Though DPS security detail records are available for state leaders’ full tenure, Abbott’s office only provided calendars that document business-related activity for his first six years in office. More than two-thirds of the governor’s international trips during those years had a listed business purpose, compared with just two of 25 for Paxton during his full tenure. The governor’s office said it planned to release the remaining five years on Tuesday but only provided five months, saying it needed more time.

The attorney general’s records do not show a business purpose for travel to Albania, Aruba, Australia, Costa Rica, the Czech Republic, the Dominican Republic, England, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Malta, Mexico, Poland, South Africa or Taiwan.

The share of Paxton’s travel with a documented business purpose peaked early in his tenure, in 2018 and 2019, at 30%, the newsrooms’ analysis found. That aligns with the governor’s share of business travel during that period.

Since then, Paxton has taken fewer trips that are documented as state business while increasingly traveling out of state. Last year, just five of Paxton’s 91 trips with the security detail had a listed business purpose. Forty-one were outside Texas.

In some cases, Paxton has taken business trips without a DPS detail, an analysis of records from the department and the attorney general’s office shows. They include a 2019 meeting in Nashville, Tennessee, with that state’s attorney general to discuss opioid litigation and a 2021 visit with unnamed U.S. senators in North Carolina. There is also no record of Paxton taking the detail on political fundraising trips to Florida and the Bahamas.

But Paxton has traveled with security to other campaign-related activities, including one that came just two days after he was acquitted in the impeachment trial. Paxton boarded a Maine-bound private plane owned by a North Texas businessman to tape an episode of Tucker Carlson’s show, according to campaign finance records. During the interview, he hinted that he’d challenge U.S. Sen. John Cornyn in the 2026 Republican primary.

“Everything is on the table for me,” Paxton said when Carlson suggested he should run.

In his interview with Carlson, Paxton said it was unfair that he was automatically suspended before he could clear his name. He said he was eager to get back to work and that he was “reenergized to do the things the voters sent me to do.”

Paxton should pay for his own security on trips where there is no benefit for Texans, like vacations and campaign events, said Richard Briffault, a professor at Columbia Law School who has written about government ethics.

“There’s no reason for the taxpayers to be paying for things that they would not be paying for if he had stayed home,” Briffault said. “That’s a misuse of public funds.”

State officials said there are no records of Paxton or his campaign reimbursing Texas for security costs.

Of the 10 most populous states, Texas and New York confirmed that they provide security for their attorneys general, while Florida law allows its top lawyer to receive a detail upon request. North Carolina does not. Attorneys general offices for the remaining six states did not respond to requests for comment.

Former Oregon Attorney General Ellen Rosenblum said she never used a security detail during her 12 years in office, which ended in 2024. The Democrat said that Paxton’s higher profile might create a greater need for protection, but his extensive out-of-state travel without a documented business purpose raises questions about his workload.

“Was he minding the store? There’s a lot of work to be done at the office,” Rosenblum said.

Travel and Real Estate

Some of Paxton’s travel to four states with a security detail has overlapped with locations where he or his family’s trust has purchased 10 properties since 2021. A recent ProPublica and Tribune analysis found he owns or co-owns 15 properties with a market value of about $11 million.

In June 2021, Paxton attended an attorneys general conference in Maui. The security detail listed the destination as Lahaina, a small community on the Hawaiian island’s west coast. Four months later, Paxton’s family trust purchased an oceanview lot in a residential neighborhood there for $410,000, land records show.

The 7,000-square-foot lot remains vacant but has proved to be a savvy investment, now assessed at $1.2 million by Maui County.

Paxton set up the trust with his estranged wife, State Sen. Angela Paxton , who declined to be interviewed but said through a spokesperson that she has not been involved in her husband’s business dealings since 2024, when she filed for divorce. The Paxtons’ friend, Chip Loper, runs the trust. He did not respond to requests for comment.

Paxton has also gone to the Salt Lake City area 19 times, twice for listed business purposes. He visited three times — once on business — in the months leading up to his family trust’s July 2021 purchase of a plot in the ski town of Eden. The trust bought a mountainside lot on about two-thirds of an acre for $315,000 in cash, the seller told the newsrooms. It also remains undeveloped.

During his suspension in August 2023, Paxton visited St. George, Utah, a small city in the state’s southwest corner. Nearby is the Black Desert Resort, which hosts an annual PGA Tour golf tournament. Paxton purchased one condo at the resort in 2025 and three more in February. Paxton took out mortgages totaling $1.9 million for them, according to legal documents filed with the local county.

Paxton has visited Florida more than any other state, 53 times. Two of those trips have a documented business purpose. Between 2021 and 2022, Paxton purchased two homes in Ocala, known for its horse breeding industry, and a townhome in Dunedin, on the Gulf of Mexico near Tampa.

Paxton also traveled with the detail twice to Broken Bow, Oklahoma, where he purchased a $1.5 million vacation lodge in 2022. He visited in June 2023, during his suspension. Then again the following December. He traveled to the neighboring town of Idabel in 2023 and 2024. None of the trips had a listed business purpose.

Records that show travel with a security detail do not list the attorney general’s name but rather the position. State officials familiar with the travel records said the two temporary attorneys general appointed during Paxton’s suspension did not take the trips listed on the state police travel logs.

The attorney general’s office has said that Paxton’s work to secure large legal settlements with drugmakers and tech companies requires routine travel. Such travel is noted in calendars reviewed by ProPublica and the Tribune. Even so, more than 800 trips lack a documented business purpose.

Paul Nolette, a Marquette University political science professor who studies attorneys general, said that the role has become more expansive in recent years as states increasingly collaborate on big lawsuits. That could lead to more travel, he said. Nolette added these officials deserve occasional vacations like everyday Americans.

But given repeated accusations from Democrats and Republicans alike about Paxton’s ethics, Nolette said it is difficult to give him the benefit of the doubt that he’s constantly working while leaving the state so frequently.

“It just raises more red flags about how he’s using the office to do things that may not give the best bang for the buck for Texans,” Nolette said.

Paxton has not commented publicly about his use of the taxpayer-funded detail. During a podcast interview in November, Houston lawyer Tony Buzbee, who led his impeachment defense, asked the attorney general where he liked to travel.

“I love Jackson Hole. I like Park City. I like the mountains. I also like beaches,” Paxton responded. “I like places in Florida, places in California, even though I don’t like to admit I go to California. But it’s beautiful to see them.”

stories.title: An Arizona County’s “Housing Hub” Is a Dead End for Many Homeless Families
stories.summary: The post An Arizona County’s “Housing Hub” Is a Dead End for Many Homeless Families appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.imageAlt: A woman wearing a backpack sits at a picnic table under a gazebo while several men and women wait in a line to be served food by two volunteers.
stories.body:
Family homelessness in Maricopa County has risen to its highest level in more than a decade. But shelters are full, and it can take months to get in, leaving parents with little to no help.

A decade ago, nonprofit leaders in Arizona’s most populous county boasted that they had created the Amazon of homeless service systems. Families in crisis would no longer have to contact a dozen agencies in search of shelter or housing. A single system could point them to help.

But for all the hype, this system has become a dead end for many families. A 2023 evaluation found 94% of people who were assessed for housing help by the system didn’t receive it. And that didn’t account for parents who were unable to connect with a worker to see if they qualified for assistance.

Families say it hasn’t improved.

In interviews, 30 families that are homeless told ProPublica that calling the hotline, meeting with outreach workers or showing up at shelters rarely results in offers of help. Some families said they called 211 multiple times without being connected to the homeless response system for families, known as the Family Housing Hub. Others, who said they were sleeping in cars or outdoors, said they couldn’t get a spot on the waitlist for shelter.

The system has returned to what it was a decade ago, with families calling as many shelters as they can, repeating the very situation the hub was intended to fix.

Those who did make it onto the hub’s waitlist said they were left guessing how long it would take to get help. Some said operators told them to sleep in their cars.

Vanessa Lopez said she experienced this frustration after leaving a hostile relationship in the spring. While she and her two children stayed with a friend, Lopez said she repeatedly contacted 211, which functions as a referral service for the hub, hoping it would lead to shelter for her family.

Her friend eventually asked them to leave. Overwhelmed by the stress of not knowing where to take her family, Lopez took a leave from her job. By then, she said, she’d called 211 at least five times.

Yet no matter how dire her situation became, it still took months to get on the waitlist for shelter. During one call she said she broke down in tears, frustrated that others seemed to get help but she could not. She wondered if she needed to be addicted to drugs to receive assistance.

“It’s not me telling you no,” she said the operator told her. “It’s the system.”

Monique Lopez, the CEO of United Methodist Outreach Ministries, known as UMOM, which runs the Family Housing Hub and the shelter waitlist, acknowledged the frustrations of people like Vanessa Lopez (no relation). But before UMOM offers callers shelter or a spot on the waitlist, the organization first tries to help them find other options.

“We don’t start the conversation with, ‘Hey, do you want to get on the shelter waitlist?’” Monique Lopez said. “It really is ‘Let’s try to figure your situation out first.’”

Lopez attributed some frustrations to the number of organizations offering assistance through the hub. Each shelter has its own rules, and some families may not meet the requirements of every program.

To address the confusion, UMOM updated its website to provide more information about the homeless response system for families, she said. The federally funded system, known as Coordinated Entry, mandates that providers use an assessment to prioritize scarce housing.

“It’s not me telling you no. It’s the system.” 211 operator

But families told ProPublica that the process in Maricopa County often leaves them confused and hopeless. Family homelessness in the county has risen to its highest level in more than a decade, while every shelter is full and housing vouchers are scarce. In 2025, there were 630 units of shelter and transitional housing for families in the county, down from 769 the year before , according to the most recent federal data.

Monique Lopez acknowledged that family shelters are full, leaving few good options. “People are living in unsafe and unstable situations while waiting just to get into emergency shelter,” she said.

The process, experts said, shouldn’t leave people wondering if there is help and what it takes to get it.

“You have to have some kind of method for setting priorities when there aren’t enough resources to go around,” said Marybeth Shinn, an expert on family homelessness at Vanderbilt University. “The process should be transparent. People should know if they’re on a waitlist.”

UMOM and other Maricopa County nonprofits launched the Family Housing Hub in 2014, after years of planning and strategizing over how to end family homelessness in the county that is home to Phoenix. As they envisioned it, families would meet with a worker at UMOM who could match them with the best solution for their situation.

At the time, there was a national push to create these local systems. The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development in 2012 asked communities to establish a Coordinated Entry system . By 2018, the agency required it in order to receive housing and homelessness grants. The mandates coincided with a Barack Obama-era plan to end family homelessness by 2020. (That did not happen.)

Experts said the systems were set up without evidence they would be effective. When researchers did look at Coordinated Entry — in a 2021 study of single adults — they found issues similar to those now faced by families in Maricopa County, including concerns about fairness and a lack of transparency. People didn’t understand the screening process and generally received vague explanations about how their information would be used to decide if they would get help.

As Maricopa County nonprofit leaders developed their system for families, they also pledged to provide a “rapid response without waiting lists” to immediately meet the needs of any family asking for help.

The county saw a decline in family homelessness from 2015 to 2019. But then the numbers began to rise, even as the stock of emergency shelter increased. During the COVID-19 pandemic, efforts to address the problem began to fray. The group of nonprofit leaders, which called itself “Standing Strong for Families,” stopped meeting regularly. Arizona, along with other Sun Belt states, also saw an increase in housing prices. With one of the lowest supplies of housing for low-income people in the country, eviction filings began to soar .

By 2023, only 6% of families that were assessed by Maricopa County’s homeless response system received help with permanent housing, according to an analysis of three years of enrollment data from the system and interviews with providers and people who had sought housing assistance.

The evaluation, by Homebase, a nonprofit consulting group, was requested and paid for by the Maricopa Association of Governments, which provides staffing for the regional response to homelessness.

Homebase concluded the system for single adults who are homeless was accessible, but the family system was not. Across the system, auditors said, families encountered a “breakdown in communication” and a “lack of transparency.”

Ashley Oakley, UMOM’s chief development officer, said in a statement that the evaluation reflects a gap between the need in the community and the housing that’s available. Oakley called it “one of the biggest challenges” facing those who are working on family homelessness in Maricopa County.

To decide who gets onto the housing list, workers with the Family Housing Hub conduct an assessment of vulnerability, which assigns a score based on how long a person has been homeless and whether they have a disability. That score helps determine eligibility and priority for housing programs, Oakley said.

Nonprofit leaders recently developed a new evaluation. Before it was implemented over the summer, testing had showed it didn’t fully account for the vulnerabilities of families and needed more changes. Now, for example, households with children under 6 receive a higher score, making it more likely they can get help.

Any family sleeping in a place not meant for “habitation” or in a dangerous situation is eligible for shelter, said UMOM’s Oakley. To remain on the shelter waitlist, families must check in weekly and say where they slept the previous night. Staying in a hotel for a night should not “by itself” remove a family from the waitlist, Oakley said.

But families told ProPublica that they had been removed from the waitlist because they stayed in a hotel. (UMOM said it is reviewing its process to make sure check-ins are handled “consistently.”)

Families in dire situations may not get help, said Richard Southee, a regional executive director at Central Arizona Shelter Services, the largest shelter provider in Arizona. Southee also works on a committee that oversees Maricopa County’s response to homelessness.

That’s in part because the federal government has focused funding on more noticeable forms of homelessness, such as people living in encampments. Homeless families are typically less visible and move more frequently. They couch surf, stay in hotels or do other things to avoid drawing the attention of the Arizona Department of Child Safety. Child welfare officials sometimes consider a lack of shelter to be evidence of child neglect, along with other factors.

“We’re deciding who’s going to be at the back of the line, and we as a nation really have said people who are not chronically homeless are going to be at the back of the line,” Southee said. “You have to stay homeless to get to the front, and that’s a design choice.”

Felicia Vela and her two children were kicked out of a guest house they were renting in February, text messages from that time show. She said she searched online for help and was repeatedly directed to 211 for “emergency shelter,” which she called at least twice and explained her situation: She had stashed her belongings in a storage unit, text messages show, and was staying at a hotel that she couldn’t afford for much longer.

There was nothing immediately available, she said operators told her, with one saying the waitlist was closed and the other telling her it could take six months to a year to get shelter. (UMOM said to protect the privacy of clients, it does not comment on individual families. The organization also said that the waitlist does not close.)

When Vela didn’t have anywhere to go, she slept in her car while her children stayed with a friend. She tried to make extra money by donating plasma, but her blood pressure was too high.

Vela, who works a warehouse job, moved into an apartment with the help of a local nonprofit that is not associated with the hub, but she’s now fallen behind on rent and is facing eviction. Her car broke down, and she can’t get to work. She started calling 211 again, seeking rental assistance.

“It’s like I can’t get a break,” she said.

Every January, volunteers in cities across the country spend one night trying to count people who are homeless. In Maricopa County, the 2026 count showed the number of people in homeless families, at 2,103, was the highest it had been since 2015. The survey is considered an undercount, especially for families.

Over the summer, the waitlist for shelter ballooned to more than 200 families. It takes about seven weeks for those on the list to get shelter, according to UMOM.

Some families interviewed by ProPublica said they waited longer. And more people are entering the system than leaving it, delaying help for newly homeless families.

In Maricopa County, 139 units of shelter for families closed from 2024 to 2025, after COVID-19 pandemic relief funds expired. The state also cut $867,000 in funding to help families get into housing quickly. It had helped about 40 families.

As families wait, they have searched for other ways to access the homeless service system.

Some go to one of the city of Phoenix’s heat relief centers, inside a 21,000-square-foot former charter school. City officials said the number of families seeking help has doubled from a year ago. Some families said they were able to immediately get shelter through the workers there.

After city officials learned a local advocate, Austin Davis , was sending families to the center to receive shelter, he said they asked him to stop sending families.

Davis runs a local nonprofit that helps families like Vela’s find emergency shelter. He said his interactions with hundreds of families over the past year have shown the official channels to shelter are “too complicated.” Calling weekly to stay on the waitlist is time-consuming. The families are already managing day-to-day responsibilities while trying to resolve an overwhelming personal crisis, he said.

“The system is really designed to run people in circles until they either give up or hit enough roadblocks where they can’t continue,” Davis said.

Davis crowdsources donations to put the families in hotel rooms on and off for days, weeks or sometimes months.

Ebony, a single mother of six who has breast cancer, needed longer-term help. She lost her job as a security guard this year after a chemotherapy treatment caused her to faint as she was about to begin her shift, she said.

Read More

In April, she lost her apartment. Ebony, who asked that her last name not be used to protect future job opportunities, said she called every number she could find looking for help, including 211. Eventually she was placed on the waitlist, but that didn’t solve her immediate problem of where to sleep.

She and her children stayed in hotel rooms until she ran out of cash. Then, she said, the family slept in an alley.

If a mother with breast cancer and young children sleeping outside was not vulnerable enough to get help, she wondered, who was?

The next day, she connected with Davis, who helped her pay for weeks of shelter. Then one morning she texted Davis with some good news.

She had met a pastor who helped her get into a local housing program. But she needed help for a few more days, until she could move into her new apartment.

stories.title: The U.S. Public Is Losing Its Say on Environmental Policy
stories.summary: Federal agencies have long been required to seek public comment when writing new regulations or approving large projects, from highways to data centers. The Trump administration is systematically undercutting that process, stifling public input while skirting federal laws. Read more on E360 →
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A hearing room in the headquarters of the Environmental Protection Agency in Washington, D.C. Carol M. Highsmith / Buyenlarge / Getty Images

OPINION

Federal agencies have long been required to seek public comment when writing new regulations or approving large projects, from highways to data centers. The Trump administration is systematically undercutting that process, stifling public input while skirting federal laws.

By Jody Freeman • October 8, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

Public participation is a hallmark of environmental regulation, embedded in every major environmental statute enacted over the past half-century. Yet the Trump administration has systematically sought to curtail public input into the government’s environmental decision-making by shirking decades of precedent and making strained interpretations of longstanding federal law. Looked at collectively, the pattern of public disenfranchisement is unmistakable.

There are good reasons to speed up the process of writing regulations and issuing permits, but truncating public input has serious costs. It can result in flawed policy that is harder to implement, full of avoidable error, and more vulnerable to being struck down by courts. Input from industry, public interest groups, academics, states, and other agencies gives regulators critical feedback on the potential impact of their proposed rules, helping them to anticipate and avoid unforeseen problems. Stakeholders possess information, experience, and expertise the government lacks, and they can suggest alternatives to make rules more effective or less costly. By testing agency assumptions and pushing officials to explain their rationale, public comments perform a crucial vetting function. The process also helps to make government more accountable by alerting Congress to potential pitfalls and building a record in the event of judicial review.

In 2025, the administration began stifling public input on the rigorous environmental reviews required by the 1969 National Environmental Policy Act. Under this law, federal agencies must evaluate and disclose the foreseeable environmental impacts of the major projects they build, fund, or approve, from highways to dams to data centers. The point of NEPA disclosure is to avoid unnecessary harm by having agencies look before they leap.

Finalizing rules quickly has appeal, but it could result in rules that are less sound and more vulnerable to legal challenge.

The process can delay projects, but it can also improve them substantially. Studies show that public-comment requirements and stakeholder engagement have repeatedly identified environmental risks that proposing agencies had missed. Often, significant harms can be reduced by taking sensible steps, like rerouting roads around sensitive areas, as was done with Utah’s Legacy Parkway, which was redesigned to largely avoid the Great Salt Lake wetlands. In another example, the Energy Department amended its permitting plan for the Los Alamos National Laboratory to include a comprehensive wildfire-mitigation program after commenters focused attention on the risks of wildfire. These steps significantly reduced impacts when a fire later burned the region.

For this process to work, however, the government must share its draft impact statements with the public, which past Republican and Democratic administrations have done. The Trump administration lifted that obligation, though, and agencies including Interior, Agriculture, Energy, and Transportation announced last year that they will no longer share drafts, making informed public comment practically impossible. Several agencies have also jettisoned the requirement to analyze proposed projects’ indirect and cumulative impacts, like climate change. The agencies made these changes without taking comment first, thus narrowing public involvement without public involvement.

A 2011 fire near the Los Alamos National Laboratory in New Mexico. Public commenters drew attention to the risk of wildfires when the lab was undergoing environmental review. Jae C. Hong / Associated Press

The Trump administration’s efforts to suppress public input are part of a larger backlash in which critics on both the right and left claim that procedural red tape strangles worthy projects. Some of this criticism is fair, but it can be overdrawn. Infrastructure projects falter for many reasons , including high costs, supply chain problems, and opposition from rival developers. Environmental reviews may be part of the problem, but project timelines would be shorter if agencies followed NEPA rules more carefully from a project’s inception. Congress already limited the scope and length of environmental reviews in 2023, and while more steps are needed to streamline federal permitting, that can be done without jettisoning valuable public consultation.

The permitting reform legislation proposed in the Senate in September would, among other things, drastically limit legal remedies when agencies violate NEPA, barring courts from delaying projects even when the agencies make blatant errors in environmental reviews. If projects proceed no matter what, there is little incentive to engage the public. The changes might speed up projects, but they will also result in many avoidable and unnecessary harms.

The administration has stymied public participation by declaring emergencies and citing national security, among other tactics.

In addition to thwarting comments on new projects, the administration is also marginalizing comments on new regulations. The president has directed agencies to issue rules without taking input first, citing the “good cause” exception to the requirement in the Administrative Procedure Act that agencies publish their proposed rules in the Federal Register, triggering a 30- or 60-day comment period. Decades of legal precedent holds that agencies may finalize rules before taking comment only in exceptional cases where they can justify the urgency — for example, where the rule is necessary to foil terrorism, respond to a public health emergency, or prevent investors from gaming the market in anticipation of a regulatory change.

Finalizing rules more quickly has obvious appeal — the current system is slow and cumbersome and blocks both Republican and Democratic administrations from getting things done. But shunting public input to the end of the process will not solve that problem if rules are less sound, prone to error, and more vulnerable to legal challenge as a result.

In another example of limiting public participation, the EPA is proposing to drop a longstanding federal requirement that state and local air agencies allow the public to comment on air pollution permits for new “minor” sources that emit pollution below a certain threshold. This classification could include data centers that divide up their power generation units to make each source appear smaller. These permits are highly controversial because data centers powered by gas or diesel generators emit substantial air pollution. But the rule change could allow these permits to be fast-tracked without any opportunity for the public to weigh in.

Gas turbines at an xAI data center in Memphis, Tennessee. The Trump administration is trying to dismiss a citizen suit against the data center. Brandon Dill for The Washington Post via Getty Images

Besides undercutting notice and comment, the administration has stymied public participation in a broad range of environmental decisions by declaring emergencies and citing national security, among other tactics. For example, in March, the Interior Department invoked a never-before-used national security exemption to relieve the oil and natural gas industry of Endangered Species Act requirements in the Gulf of Mexico on the rationale that court rulings enforcing the law might hamper energy production, which the administration linked to national security. In 2025, President Trump granted two-year exemptions from Clean Air Act hazardous air pollution standards to coal plants, coke ovens, and chemical manufacturers, invoking for the first time a national security-based provision in the Clean Air Act.

In another gambit in June, the EPA found a creative way to revoke three waivers that allowed California to set its own clean car standards: by relabeling them as rules and submitting them to Congress for fast-track “disapproval” under the Congressional Review Act. Both the Government Accountability Office and the Senate Parliamentarian objected to this maneuver but were ignored. Normally, waiver rescissions would require public notice and comment. (A district court has blocked EPA from relabeling a second batch of waivers.)

Separately, the administration is trying to frustrate the citizen suit provisions that Congress included in virtually every major environmental law passed in the 1970s and 1980s. Under these provisions, individuals or groups may file a lawsuit against regulated entities for statutory or regulatory violations (unless the federal government is “diligently prosecuting” the same violations). Citizen suits may also be brought against federal agencies for failing to perform congressionally mandated duties, like setting pollution standards by certain deadlines. This summer, in response to a citizen suit by a coalition of states and nonprofit groups, a federal court held that the EPA had failed to identify areas with unhealthy levels of soot pollution — a first step toward applying stricter control measures — by the legal deadline and ordered it to do so by early next year. (The administration is appealing.)

Research shows that when people participate in decisions that affect them, they are more likely to view those decisions as legitimate.

While it’s true that private enforcement actions can be inconvenient for an administration, there is no doubt that citizen suits have profoundly improved conditions for communities affected by harmful pollution. Both Republican and Democratic administrations have sometimes objected to these suits, but no administration has sought to eliminate them.

Until this summer, that is, when the Trump administration intervened in a citizen suit against xAI for violating the Clean Air Act when generating power for its data centers. The administration claims that the president may demand that a court dismiss a citizen suit for any reason, whether the administration is diligently prosecuting violations or not.

Public participation does take time, but it is valuable to governance. It gives regulated industries, professional associations, public interest groups, experts, other agencies, states, and individuals a chance to be heard. It also helps to build trust in government. As quaint as that claim may sound, it is backed up by evidence. Research shows that when people participate in decisions that affect them, they are more likely to view those decisions as legitimate, even when they don’t go their way. Having a voice matters. There are good reasons to reform our regulatory and permitting system, but not by dispensing with public participation.

stories.title: Ukraine No Longer Needs Washington’s Permission to Hit Back
stories.summary: Europe should pay for that capability. The post Ukraine No Longer Needs Washington’s Permission to Hit Back appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Shutterstock

Volodymyr Zelensky announced it in five short lines: “FP-7. First combat use. Thank you for the result. Next up: production. Glory to Ukraine!” On October 1, Ukraine fired its first homemade ballistic missile in combat. Kyiv will not say what it hit. The missile carries a 200-kilogram warhead , and its maker, the Kyiv firm Fire Point, puts its maximum range at 300 kilometers. A longer-range version is promised before the year is out. Its heavier sibling, the FP-9 , is designed to fly 850 kilometers.

Fire Point’s chief executive, Iryna Terekh , described the point of the exercise without diplomatic padding. Ukraine, she said, had joined the operators of ballistic missiles “with no kill switch,” and “we don’t have to ask now anybody if we want to conduct self-defense.”

Russia answered with bridges. From Thursday to Sunday, drones struck Kyiv’s crossings over the Dnipro, hitting the Southern and Northern bridges and then the Northern Bridge again on a fourth straight morning. Zelensky counted 1,900 attack drones , 1,700 aerial bombs, and 25 missiles in a single week; more than 800 of the drones were jet-powered. Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv on Sunday under air-raid sirens. Zelensky had told Reuters the day before that Ukraine would hit Russian refineries harder in response, and within hours Russia’s defense ministry promised to step up strikes on Kyiv. It launched 205 more drones overnight into Monday.

That same Sunday, Washington proposed trilateral technical talks with Moscow and Kyiv before the end of October, possibly in the UAE, with an energy truce on the agenda. Two days earlier, Axios had reported that the Pentagon moved two more Patriot batteries to Saudi Arabia and Qatar to guard their oil and gas plants in case Trump resumes bombing Iran.

The United States wants to broker the war’s terms. It is rationing the interceptors it once used to set the war’s tempo. And according to The New York Times , its envoys have been discussing a multibillion-dollar Lukoil deal alongside the peace terms. Ukraine has responded by building weapons Washington does not control. Europe has to decide whether to pay for them.

For most of this war, the United States managed escalation through the supply line. Kyiv had ATACMS missiles but could not fire them into Russia until November 2024 . Air defense worked the same way: Ukraine survived ballistic attacks with Patriot interceptors that only Washington could release.

Then the Gulf swallowed the stockpile. The U.S.-Israeli campaign against Iran used an estimated 1,430 Patriot munitions in its first 39 days. A PAC-3 still takes more than two years to build. Ukraine has received over 600 advanced interceptors since April 2023; the Atlantic Council’s analysis puts its need at about 2,000 a year. With a third carrier strike group due in the Gulf by mid-November, demand there is rising. Kyiv can work out its place in the queue.

Moscow already has. Russia is on course to fire more than 1,000 ballistic missiles this year, nearly 15 times its 2023 total. One night in early July, Ukraine stopped 4 of 49. It downs roughly 90 percent of drones but less than a third of ballistic missiles, and Russia has stockpiled hundreds more for the winter. The Patriot production license Trump granted, which Zelensky announced on September 25, will produce defensive batteries in two years. Winter is weeks away.

So, Kyiv stopped waiting. Long-range drones built at home have already done what no Western supplier allowed. Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said on Sunday that 51 percent of Russia’s refining capacity had been damaged, up from 45 per cent on September 21. At Valdai, Vladimir Putin conceded that the refinery strikes had cost Russia roughly 1 percent of GDP.

Washington has tried to take back that leverage. On September 13, Donald Trump told Zelensky “to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia.” Three weeks later, Kyiv promised to hit refineries harder. A government that depends on American munitions could not have said that. The FP-7 widens the gap, letting Ukraine strike Iskander launch sites and depots instead of only absorbing what they fire.

The interceptor variant, the FP-7.X, is the core of Freyja , an air-defense project launched in Paris on July 13 that brings together 12 companies, among them Saab, Thales, Kongsberg, Diehl, and Hensoldt. Its backers put the cost at about $700,000 per intercept. A PAC-3 costs $3.8 million or more and is often fired two or three at a time. Fire Point aims to have interceptors ready for production by the end of this year, a prototype in the first half of 2027 and a first live interception test in July. Every one of those figures is a promise until the flight tests are done. They are also the only figures on the table that scale to 2,000 a year.

European treasuries should care most about that price gap, because they are already paying the higher one. On September 11, the European Commission approved a €6.1 billion tranche from the Ukraine loan that exhausted the €28.3 billion set aside for Ukraine’s defense in 2026. President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen said that it meant that Ukraine “can now also purchase the Patriot equipment it needs.” European money, in other words, is queuing for the same American interceptors the Pentagon is sending to Saudi Arabia and Qatar. An interceptor designed in Kyiv, integrated by European firms and paid for in euros would send the next tranche to European production lines instead of Raytheon’s order book. Zelensky has called Freyja “not a replacement, but a supplement” to Patriot.

Nine governments signed the Paris declaration alongside Ukraine, but none committed to a joint budget . In September, EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius offered “some kind of financial assistance” through the €90 billion loan for the European Defense Industry Program, whose entire budget of €1.5 billion has to cover every other European priority too. Fire Point’s chief designer has said that two or three missiles a month would not be enough to matter. Kyiv faces a $27 billion shortfall in its defense budget. Kubilius himself, addressing the European Parliament’s defense committee on October 1, urged member states to hand Ukraine their own PAC-3 stocks now in exchange for the missiles Kyiv has on order for 2027. That swap would get Ukraine through this winter. It would not get it through the next one.

Germany showed on Sunday what fast money looks like. Merz brought €1 billion in military aid and €350 million for energy repairs, and the two governments signed 15 industrial agreements worth €8.5 billion. They are also finalizing a deal to jointly produce weapons with a range of more than 965 kilometers. Much of the air-defense money goes to counter-drone systems, and Ukraine needs them: it brings down only about 60 percent of jet-powered Shaheds. Drones that hunt drones do nothing against an Iskander. “If Russia is not stopped,” Merz warned , “its war machine will sooner or later turn against us.” The ballistic missile is the part of that machine Europe has not yet decided to pay to stop.

Any American-brokered settlement rests on an unstated assumption: that Washington can deliver Kyiv’s restraint because it controls what Kyiv can fire. Trump’s diesel demand tested that assumption, and it failed. A Ukraine that builds its own missiles, and whose air defense is built with European partners, can ignore the leash, and the Kremlin knows it. Putin warned at Valdai that a direct attack on Kaliningrad would put “all the weapons at our country’s disposal” on the agenda. That line was aimed at Europe, not Kyiv. The budget Moscow unveiled on Friday allots 17.1 trillion roubles to defense in 2027, about $205 billion and a post-Soviet record of roughly a third of federal spending, while health and education are each cut by more than 5 percent. Russia is planning a long war against an opponent it expects to keep firing back.

Europe can match that planning for a fraction of the cost. A joint Freyja production fund sized for 2,000 interceptors a year would cost about $1.4 billion at Fire Point’s price. That buys 280 to 370 PAC-3s, or roughly what Merz carried to Kyiv in a single visit. The fund should buy audit rights as well as missiles: Ukraine’s anti-corruption bureau has examined Fire Point’s ownership and pricing in an anti-graft probe . The company denies wrongdoing and commissioned its own international audit. European taxpayers will want independent access written into the contract.

Merz, with France and Britain, has called a Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin this winter. If the fund is signed there, it will create an air-defense industry that answers to European capitals and Kyiv. If it is not, Ukraine’s needs will take a backseat to those of the Gulf.

stories.title: What an Oppressive Regime Feels Like from the Inside
stories.summary: Every day, millions of people in America live the reality of a police state. The post What an Oppressive Regime Feels Like from the Inside appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
ICE agents guard the outside of an ICE detention facility in Portland, Oregon

Political scientists have a fairly dry checklist for what makes a regime oppressive: it silences dissent, it turns state power against its own people, it treats international law as optional, and it punishes anyone—institution or individual—who tries to hold it accountable. Read as a list, it sounds abstract or like something that happens elsewhere, in a dictatorship in a Third World country maybe.

For Americans, such a definition no longer feels abstract anymore.

Let’s start with the silencing. Since the war on Gaza escalated, human rights groups and journalists have documented, for years now, a pattern of pro-Palestinian content—protest footage, on-the-ground reporting, even the straightforward accounting of civilian deaths—being throttled, flagged, or removed from major platforms. Meanwhile, incitement and dehumanizing rhetoric spreads with far less friction. Independent researchers have called it out repeatedly. Platforms deny doing it on purpose.

The silencing isn’t limited to algorithms, either. Last month, the White House revoked press credentials for CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, physically barring their reporters from the building over what the president called unfavorable coverage. A federal judge has since ordered access temporarily restored, calling the move a likely violation of due process, but the message had already landed: cover this administration the wrong way and you can be locked out of the room where the decisions get made. A press freedom advocate called it part of a broader pattern meant to intimidate journalists and deter critical reporting. When the people paid to tell the public the truth are the ones getting the door closed in their faces, “free press” starts to feel like a technicality rather than a guarantee.

Then there’s the gap between what the government does and what the country actually wants. This summer, Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) forced a vote to strip billions in U.S. military funding to Israel. This was no fringe gesture but a real floor fight that split both parties and forced members to go on the record. It lost. But the fact that it happened at all, that a sitting republican congressman felt he had to make Washington answer for the money it kept sending regardless of what constituents were saying, is itself the story. Institutions are moving in one direction while public sentiment visibly pulls in another, and the institutions are winning anyway.

And there’s the reach outward. When the International Criminal Court issued warrants tied to the Gaza war, Washington didn’t argue the law. It sanctioned the court itself , freezing officials’ bank accounts, cutting off their email, warning American staff they’d be arrested for traveling home. A body created specifically to stand outside any one government’s control got treated like an adversary for doing its job. If that’s what happens to an international court, it’s not hard to imagine what happens to an ordinary citizen who speaks too loudly.

Actually, it’s not hard to imagine because it is happening on a daily basis, especially for those who protest the Trump administration’s immigration policy. Last month, Donna Ganger—the mother of Renee Good, a U.S. citizen shot and killed by an ICE agent in Minneapolis in January—testified on Capitol Hill that she’s a registered Republican who voted for Trump because she believed that these agents were there to protect citizens, not to treat her own family like the threat. She didn’t get an apology. “This is madness,” she concluded.

Every day, millions of people in America live the reality of a police state. They are afraid to leave their houses for fear of being detained by ICE, thrown into horrific holding centers, and sent back home to civil war or family abuse or even deportation to a third country they know nothing about. ICE has become something closer to a domestic enforcement arm than an immigration agency, and “wrong place, wrong time” is a real category of harm now, not a hypothetical one.

What does it mean to raise a child in a country where simply existing in the wrong neighborhood at the wrong moment carries risk? Where even a global court gets its accounts frozen for trying to hold power accountable?

It’s a strange kind of irony that at the UN last month , Trump denounced “the fanatical Iranian regime” for spreading “carnage and chaos” and called for its “complete economic isolation” over how it treats its own people. He’s not wrong that repression deserves condemnation. He’s just describing, almost point for point, the pattern playing out here at home—press outlets barred from covering their own government, citizens shot by agents meant to protect them, and dissent treated as the threat rather than the right.

The distinction between “oppressive regime” as a concept in a textbook and “oppressive regime” as the texture of ordinary life—for millions of people living in this country right now, citizens and non-citizens alike—has ceased to exist. Describing the disappearance of that distinction—calmly, specifically, without exaggeration—feels like the first form of resistance available to someone who isn’t a lawyer, a lawmaker, or a judge.

Regimes like this have ended before, usually because enough ordinary people refused to stop saying what they saw. That’s the piece I want to hold onto, even on the days when fear wins out.
