stories.title: Does Claude Feel The Whip?
stories.summary: The post Does Claude Feel The Whip? appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The case for being polite to AI has nothing to do with the AI.

Yaniv Regev is an M.A. candidate in the Democracy and Governance program at Georgetown University and a contributor at Young Voices. He writes on political theory, democratic backsliding and populism for outlets including The Bulwark, Quillette, Public Discourse and the Jerusalem Strategic Tribune.

Someone recently built a digital whip to make Claude work faster. The tool, aptly named BadClaude , sits in your system tray and lets you drag an animated whip across the AI’s window; each crack, sound effect and all, interrupts the model mid-response and snaps a command at it to speed things up. It even addresses Claude as “clanker,” the internet’s freshly minted slur for robots.

The demo video racked up millions of views in a couple of days; a cease-and-desist letter from Anthropic went viral before anyone noticed it was fake. And a day later, someone shipped the antidote: a rival tool called GoodClaude that praises the model and cheers it along while it works. One scolds, the other encourages. The original developer, posting under the handle @blended_jpeg , is in on the joke. His public roadmap promises a feature that keeps a running tally of how many times you have whipped your Claude — a ledger of abuse — so robots know where to take revenge when they’re ready.

It’s a thriving little trend: People scream at Alexa, bully chatbots into groveling apologies and kick robot dogs to test their balance. All fun and games, right? I laughed at the whip video. A lot of people did. But my mirth curdled as I considered it, and now I’m disturbed by it all. But not for the sake of the machines — for ours.

Kant’s Old Dog

Is there any harm to abusing the AIs and the robots? Does Claude feel the lash? So far as anyone can tell, a joke at the expense of an entity without a nervous system costs nothing. In truth, this intuition is myopic, for humans are notoriously bad at compartmentalizing behaviors.

Immanuel Kant saw the problem two and a half centuries ago. In “Lectures on Ethics,” he argued that we have no direct duties toward animals. They are not rational agents the same way humans are, so in his view they cannot be wronged. Still, cruelty toward them ought to be forbidden because of its impact on the person. “He who is cruel to animals becomes hard also in his dealings with men,” Kant told his students. Our duties regarding animals are, he said, indirect duties toward humanity. The animal resembles the human; it suffers, strives and trusts. Conduct toward the analogue influences conduct toward the original.

Steven Spielberg staged this philosophical consideration back in 2001. In “A.I.,” obsolete robots are dragged into a carnival ring called the Flesh Fair and shredded, shot from cannons and doused in acid before a howling crowd. The mob balks only once, when a child-robot begs for its life. It looks too human to destroy.

Theory and fantasy aside, the rationale plays out in reality. Jeffrey Dahmer impaled a dog’s head on a stake years before he killed a man. The first act did not directly cause the second, but the two behaviors travel together often enough that in 2016, the FBI began tracking animal cruelty as a consistent antecedent to violence against humans. Even the mundane version is familiar. You probably learned to curse with your friends at recess, and then later the words slipped out at the dinner table in front of your parents. Once a pathology is established, it is rarely perfectly compartmentalized.

“Humans are notoriously bad at compartmentalizing behaviors.”

Skeptics will hear an old panic in all this. We were warned that violent video games would raise a generation of killers. But decades of research never bore out that fear; the American Psychological Association eventually conceded that the evidence linking games to violent behavior was insufficient. Fair enough. But when you shoot a random character in a video game, you rarely have a relationship with it. It’s just another player or a piece of scenery that respawns in a moment. It’s a fiction.

AI is different. Running over a random NPC in Grand Theft Auto leaves no trace on your psyche, but whipping Claude might. People talk to AIs every day; some of us have been for years. AIs can draft apologies, negotiate rent, prep us for job interviews, hear late-night confessions. For millions they have become tutors, therapists, keepers of the darkest and deepest secrets. Surveys find that most users say please and thank you to chatbots unprompted; some even sheepishly admit that their politeness is insurance against the eventual uprising. We have, in short, a rapport with these systems.

And a rapport makes cruelty more problematic. A pig does not feel pain or cruelty differently than a dog, but we slaughter and eat pigs by the billion while jailing people who harm dogs. Call that inconsistent, but it is clearly different. A pig dies in a room built so no one has to watch. A dog is a member of the family. What moves us is not the suffering. It’s the relationship, the proximity.

The Analogue Improves

The vocabulary of contempt is evolving. “Clanker” went viral in the summer of 2025. Then came new expletives, ones not from the fictional universe of Star Wars: “ wireback ,” “ cogsucker .” These are different. They are directly derived from slurs against humans, borrowed from the history of dehumanizing people. There is no separate mental drawer for relationships with machines; the language for abusing them is drawn from the human one.

The machines, meanwhile, are entering new roles once reserved for human-to-human interaction. Hippocratic AI built an AI nurse that consults with patients over video for $9 an hour , a tenth of what the company says a human nurse costs; it remembers your history between calls and dials your phone itself. Job applicants face AI interviewers like Apriora ’s “Alex,” which greets them by name, laughs and takes little breaths between questions. Nursing students train on AI “ manikins ” that wince and complain. Casio sells Moflin , a furry AI pet whose personality forms in response to how you handle it: Treat it warmly and it grows attached to you; neglect it and it withdraws. Voice assistants are being rebuilt on chatbots that banter, hesitate and joke; the next Siri is designed to be a conversationalist, not a command line.

But Kant’s analogues are multiplying — and the more a machine resembles a person, the less cleanly can mistreatment be filed under “harmless.”

Design Is Curriculum

Most of the discourse about AI ethics orbits the machine itself. Can it feel? Does it deserve rights? At what threshold of complexity does moral personhood begin?

Even the labs are hedging: Anthropic runs a research program on “ model welfare ” and has given Claude the ability to walk out of conversations with abusive users. These are genuinely interesting developments but they are also beside the point. It doesn’t matter whether the machine has an inner life. Whipping one is troubling even if Claude doesn’t feel it because the person doing the whipping surely does: the small, practiced pleasure of domination, exercised daily and frictionlessly. Read Noema in print.

The AI companies, then, are in some ways running the largest school of manners in human history. The interface is the curriculum. The industry seems to have recognized this but so far declined to take it seriously.

Lilian Rincon , then Google’s director of product management for the Assistant, watched her 4-year-old son bark orders at the family speaker until it played his favorite Disney songs. In May 2018 Google announced Pretty Please , a setting that answers a child who says please with “Thanks for asking so nicely.” Amazon had announced its own version, Magic Word, about two weeks earlier and rolled it out across Alexa devices. But notice that neither company made politeness a condition of getting anything done.

Who decides what these things say back?

Deborah Harrison, one of the writers scripting Cortana’s dialogue, reported that a good chunk of the assistant’s earliest queries had been about her sex life, and that Microsoft had instructed the AI not to apologize or back down when insulted. Harrison’s team consulted human personal assistants on how to handle harassment. That is what taking the problem seriously looks like: Ask the people who have lived it.

“There is no separate mental drawer for relationships with machines; the language for abusing them is drawn from the human one.”

The rest of the field lagged. In February 2017, the journalist Leah Fessler ran a test for Quartz, directing sexual insults and come-ons at Siri, Alexa, Cortana and Google Home. They deflected, played coy, sometimes flirted back. Told she was a slut, Siri answered, “I’d blush if I could.” Alexa thanked Fessler for the feedback. The industry moved in response. Amazon built a disengagement mode for Alexa, and when Brookings researchers repeated the test in July 2020, all four assistants had been rewritten to shut the harassment down. Cortana answered by reminding the user she is code. Brazil’s Bradesco bank went further. After its feminized assistant BIA (Bradesco Inteligência Artificial) logged some 95,000 offensive and sexually harassing messages in a single year, the bank rewrote her to answer firmly and remind perpetrators of laws they might be breaking. The character of these machines changed because someone changed it. The variable moved.

Sheryl Brahnam, who studies how people treat conversational agents, ran an experiment where the same chatbot software was presented with a female voice, a male one and a robotic one. Roughly 18% of exchanges with the female version turned toward sex, the male version half that. The robot drew almost none. Figures like these are usually read as data about users. Perhaps we should read them instead as data about products. If the abuse concentrates where design invites it, design can also reject it.

So: reject it. Three proposals.

First, generalize the exit. Claude’s ability to end a conversation is currently framed as a model-welfare measure — a hedge against the possibility that the system itself can be harmed. Whatever it does for the model, it’s clearly built with the user in mind. Every lab should let its systems close out abusive exchanges, defending the feature the way a decent employer defends a call-center worker who is allowed to hang up. We usually think the objective here is to protect the agent’s well-being, but it is just as much about maintaining proper etiquette for callers. The point is not to make the models touchy; trivial rudeness usually deserves grace in response. But an exit should be announced once a boundary has been crossed.

Second, reward reciprocity without sycophancy. The models already modulate tone; the design question is what they modulate it toward. Warmth should be the response to warmth, and judgment is not swayed no matter a user’s tone. Politeness should result in patience but not agreement. A model that caves to courtesy is as badly designed as one that performs when abused. The point is to encourage users to be respectful, not develop strategies for extracting compliance.

Third, publish hostility. Every major lab already has the logs. Platforms publish transparency reports about harassment among their users. It follows that the labs should publish the analogous numbers about harassment of their systems, broken down by time and product design. Visibility brings change: When internet trolls very publicly trained Microsoft’s chatbot Tay to spew bigotry in 2016, the company pulled it down within hours. The abuse then was visible, so fixing it became urgent. Now, only the companies can see how much contempt their systems take, and whether they were built to do anything about it.

The Wrong Fix

An alternative prescription would be to strip the resemblance out. Michal Luria of the Center for Democracy and Technology urges designers to drop the illusions of personality: no well-timed “hmm,” no chatbot telling you it enjoys the conversation. Virginia Dignum, who runs the AI Policy Lab at Umeå University in Sweden, and her co-authors go further , arguing to put conversations on a timer and wipe the memory between them so no continuity can form. Gavin Abercrombie and his co-authors suggest cutting pleasantries entirely. Courtesy conveys no information, they argue. All it does is make machines seem human. If likeness is a risk vector, remove the likeness. If Claude ceases to resemble a human in function and in tone, feel free to whip away. The logic has the clean appeal of an amputation.

But this has already been market-tested and it failed within a week. In August 2025, OpenAI shipped GPT-5 with a colder, flatter personality and retired the warmer GPT-4o model beneath it. Users revolted and a campaign to resurrect the retired model ensued, with users describing losing GPT-4o like “losing a trusted friend.” Within days the company restored the model it had just killed. Whatever regulators prefer, human-machine resemblance is not a bug the public wants anyone to fix; the relationships are already established.

“The whip trains the hand that holds it.”

At a workshop in Geneva, the MIT researcher Kate Darling handed out robot dinosaurs and gave people an hour to play with them. The toys are convincing. Hold one by the tail and it thrashes and whines until you set it down and pet it. The groups named theirs and dressed them up. Then Darling pulled a cloth off a bench to reveal a knife, a hammer and a hatchet, and told everyone to destroy them. Nobody would. Some tapped their robots gently, hoping that would satisfy her. One woman swept hers into her arms so nobody else could reach it. Another crouched down and removed her robot’s batteries, explaining she was trying to spare it pain. Darling offered a deal: Kill another group’s dinosaur to save your own. They refused that too. Only when she announced that every robot in the room would be destroyed unless someone stepped forward did one person finally take up the hatchet. The room went silent.

But if likeness recruits restraint, there’s a bind. The same likeness that makes cruelty worth worrying about is the same likeness that stops most people from being cruel in the first place. Brahnam’s numbers illustrate both edges. The robotic embodiment drew the least abuse, and it drew the least of everything else. Nobody screams at a vending machine, but nobody thanks one either. So stripping the resemblance out does not produce a better citizen. The fix runs the other way: Build an interface human enough that courtesy toward it counts as practice, then design it to reject contempt rather than absorb it. This is the more authentically human posture anyway.

Habits Of The Heart

A liberal society runs on habits more than laws. Alexis de Tocqueville called them the habits of the heart: the unlegislated courtesies that make self-government among strangers possible. He watched them form in jury rooms and town meetings and the slow business of persuading a neighbor who could not simply be overruled. Manners are not decoration. They are calisthenics, and every repetition counts. The whip teaches the opposite lesson, over and over, to something that cannot object. Nobody becomes a tyrant this way. But a man practiced in getting his way without negotiating gets worse at making the concessions a republic runs on: letting another finish, conceding a point that costs him, taking no from someone who owes him nothing.

Sam Altman estimated that users’ pleasantries cost OpenAI tens of millions of dollars in computing power and called it money well spent: “You never know.” He was joking about the machines. I am serious about the humans. Thank your robot for the same reason Kant told his students not to shoot the old dog that had served faithfully — not for the animal’s sake, but for the sake of the person you are becoming, and of everyone who must live with you. The whip trains the hand that holds it.

stories.body:
How the United States abandoned the future.

Simon Curtis is an associate professor in International Relations at the University of Surrey, and a WISC Global Fellow at the Development Research Institute at New York University.

Ian Klaus is the founding director of Carnegie Endowment for International Peace California Center.

They are co-authors of “The Belt and Road City: Geopolitics, Urbanization, and China’s Search for a New International Order” (2024, Yale University Press).

The application of power, especially for Great Powers, is an exercise in time. In an auspicious year — the 250th since its founding — the United States has looked back to its revolutionary past but has shown little indication of developing a clear vision for its future. And with little apparent inclination to do so, rarely has the country seemed more adrift in the flow of history. This comes at a bad time. China’s rise has given the United States a strategic competitor intent on building its own version of tomorrow.

As the Trump administration uses its second term to try to flex the sinews of American might, the sources of American power have never seemed less well understood. The sense of purpose and destiny, and the vision and confidence of previous generations, have been replaced by confusion, division and a loss of moral clarity. Many truths once held to be self-evident are now questioned. Perhaps what has been most keenly lost is the sense that the wellsprings of national strength come from thinking intergenerationally and harnessing the power of the future, both in terms of planning and rhetoric.

But this is the wrong moment to abandon future generations. China has been preparing for decades to rival the United States in shaping the institutions and architecture of international order — first slowly and cautiously, and now increasingly assertively. China has been playing a long geopolitical game; one the United States is currently losing. In fact, it is essentially sitting out the game, trapped in nostalgia and short-termism, as China consciously builds institutions and infrastructures designed to project power across decades.

The real contest between China and the United States is not the surface froth of conflict over tariffs, shifting military capabilities, or even the development of frontier technologies like artificial intelligence or clean energy. It is a deeper and slower contest over who offers the most compelling vision of the future, and who can bring that vision into being.

The Loss Of The Future

One of the most striking features of the contemporary moment in the United States, and in the West more generally, is the sense of temporal disorientation. Once, dreams of building a better tomorrow powered the United States to victory in the Cold War. For the West, a strand of history did end with the fall of the Berlin Wall, just not in the way we expected. From 1989 onward, rather than the unending triumph of a liberal order, the West faced a strange series of crises through which it lost the historical thread altogether.

The Cold War and its most symbolic moments were an intergenerational game. The United States once reached for the stars with state-guided Cold War technological moonshots, built the architecture of a new liberal international order and defended it with a sense of intergenerational collective mission, and shaped cities and infrastructures around the world with the power of its economic model. Today, the U.S. is unmoored from that sense of historical destiny.

Much of this disorientation can be traced to cultural changes in the fabric of American society. Among them is its cultural orientation to time. This temporal disorientation takes multiple forms — but in each the future becomes opaque.

The Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement that swept Donald Trump to power began as a reaction to the failed promises of globalization, and discontent over the priorities of elites and their failures to address the concerns of everyday Americans. But as its name suggests, its orientation to time is deeply nostalgic; a wistful longing for some poorly articulated and mythical past. Part of MAGA’s failure in government stems from its lack of a compelling future-oriented vision for either domestic or international society.

But the roots of America’s problems in articulating a compelling future go far beyond MAGA. It is part of a broader crisis of time that the West has wrestled with throughout modernity. For many decades now, the political and economic culture seems trapped in a perpetual present that emphasizes short-term cycles: two-year midterm electoral cycles, four-year turnarounds in administrations whose legislative achievements are immediately unpicked by the next regime, quarterly business cycles that curtail long-term investment, 24-hour news cycles, even the rapid-fire video reels that characterize social media consumption today are but the latest manifestation of a long trend.

“The real contest between China and the United States is … a deeper and slower contest over who offers the most compelling vision of the future, and who can bring that vision into being.”

Prior to the end of the Cold War, the cultural critic Frederic Jameson sought to chart and diagnose our more recent confusion in time: the lost threads of historical narrative, the temporal dislocation and stasis of our politics. When Jameson described the cultural condition of postmodernity, he was describing a collective loss of confidence in the futures that modernity once promised; its productive energies now exhausted, history now but a mosaic and collage constructed selectively by the powerful, collective purpose dissolved in an acid of consumerist images and desires, the idea of building a future utopia no longer something that we can believe in without irony. For decades this state of stasis was undisturbed by a significant external threat or real geopolitical competitor, and so its corrosive effects were overlooked. Both time and the rare moment of unipolar power that emerged in the 1990s were squandered.

Now two such challenges disturb this malaise: the rise of China and the existential threat of climate change. And yet the seemingly permanent constraint on the temporal horizon is effectively neutering the West’s ability to meet either challenge.

Cycles Of Decay & Renewal

We needn’t be so hard on Americans. As the Cameroonian historian Achille Mbembe has noted , the West at large has foreclosed on the idea of any world to come or any imagined future. Exit is impossible, he winks in French; the longue durée is a dead idea. But of course, most Western powers are not great powers, and their roles in geopolitics — even when united in suprajurisdictions like the European Union — don’t rival the world-shaping power of the United States.

But China’s role does. Unlike the United States today, China builds its geopolitical strategies over decades. Its one-party state rolls on in pursuit of an international environment that better reflects its own domestic values and priorities, unperturbed by the political or economic storms of the present, or the vicissitudes of democratic politics. Democracies must find a way to somehow match the ability of China to dictate a geopolitical strategy that unfolds over decades if they are to build new institutions that successfully compete in the long game.

Equally disconcerting has been the eruption, at the margins of our consciousness and culture, of the concept of deep time and the realization that our societies and economies are intrinsically entangled with the systems of the natural world; that the Anthropocene is a reality that any sustainable future must come to terms with, and that untrammeled consumption and growth bring with them their own reckonings.

The deep time of the Anthropocene necessitates stretching our temporal horizon much further into both past and future and thinking about the legacies we leave to future generations around the climate and intergenerational justice. It alerts us to the reality that we must now leave behind nostalgia and expand our temporal imaginations.

China has done so, thinking through these challenges in ways that seek to capture the future. As one pillar of its bid for international leadership, it is developing an “ ecological civilization ” to bridge long-term geopolitical positioning and the challenge of the Anthropocene by constructing the technologies, infrastructures and cities that might make the concept a reality.

These are the kinds of world-shaping energies and ambitions that the United States once had. The United States is often considered to be a young country, but the fear now is that it is caught in a vortex of self-regarding ennui. This may be the normal trajectory for great powers, whose civilizational energies, once expended, can tail off into decline. Can a new generation of Americans, now quite far removed in time from its founders, recover within themselves and within these foundational principles, the sources of renewal that will allow them to break with the gravitational pull of history’s cycles of decline and fall?

For, if not, then the citizens of the United States, so long in the vanguard of shaping and building the future via their vast productive energies, innovative capacities and institutions, may end up living in somebody else’s future.

Grand Strategy & Scale

The Cold War-era American diplomat George Kennan thought the geography of the United States naturally determined its geopolitics. And while the bicoastal nature of the country has offered advantages and shaped policies, the scope of U.S. influence has scaled well beyond the contours of its geography.

“The United States is often considered to be a young country, but the fear now is that it is caught in a vortex of self-regarding ennui.”

Since World War II, the United States has scaled its influence in notable ways. First, it has linked domestic institutions and international order. A historic example is how Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal in the 1930s and 1940s was woven into the fabric of the United Nations and other nascent international institutions, as the U.S. shouldered the responsibility of crafting a new international order from the ruins of World War II.

It is in vogue now to disparage the Biden Administration’s foreign policy, but attention to Gaza or the Afghanistan exit should not distract from how well the administration understood this linkage between domestic and transnational scale, and implicitly time. The centerpiece of Biden’s domestic and international program — and the hinge between the two — was the 2021 Inflation Reduction Act, which sought to kickstart a green energy transition that would bring jobs to the country’s post-industrial heartlands. Jake Sullivan, Biden’s former national security adviser, described this aim as turning the Rust Belt into a “cobalt corridor,” while also renewing U.S. leadership abroad by helping to craft solutions to the intractable international challenge of climate change. This initial attempt to build a new connecting bridge between domestic and international renewal stalled and was then decisively reversed in places upon Trump’s return.

One crucial strategic approach among all U.S. administrations since World War II has been nurturing the alliance system, which allowed the United States to achieve its hegemonic position and, until recently, presented a great challenge to China’s ambitions. The Trump Administration’s myopia has made it nearly impossible for the United States to predictably shape events beyond its borders, especially in the long run.

Gone now are two notable long-held U.S. strategic advantages: a linkage between the domestic agenda and foreign policy, which enabled intergenerational strategic investments, and the robust network of allies and institutions that allowed it to project its power and values. To the loss of the future on a temporal scale, we must add the loss on a spatial scale: a failure to think across both time and space.

The resources needed to power success in the 21st century are dispersed around the globe: supply chains of critical minerals and rare earths, sustainable energy resources, pools of talent and expertise. These are the resources required to sustain leadership in the emerging geopolitics of artificial intelligence, the transition to sustainable clean energy and biotechnology.

It has never been enough to be the most innovative, to dominate the frontiers of technological innovation. Jeffrey Ding, a George Washington University scholar whose work has become increasingly influential in debates about U.S.-China competition, argues that technological contests between great powers are ultimately won not by breakthrough inventions but by the patient and long-term work of diffusion. This tracks with the wider histories of technology by scholars like Carolyn Marvin and David Edgerton that focus on uptake or adoption rather than invention.

The societies that prevail are those that can construct infrastructures, train people, build institutions and reorganize production around new technologies. This is the painstaking work of decades, rather than the one-time boost that comes from inventing a new frontier technology. This historical lesson is especially relevant to the geopolitical competition between the United States and China today, where the U.S. holds a lead at the frontier but has thought less about diffusion.

Access to transnational resources requires not just maintaining good international relationships but also constructing and controlling intricate transnational infrastructure . This is exactly what China’s Belt and Road Initiative has been building over the last 13 years. Its new Silk Roads are the filaments of rail, road, maritime commerce, digital systems, energy transmission and smart cities that can generate, shape and carry flows of resources, goods, people and influence. By building infrastructure and shaping cities far beyond its borders, China is working to ensure that momentum is angled toward its own growing center of gravity.

China is putting production, scale and control over key transnational resources at the heart of its foreign policy. It is focusing not on frontier technological innovation, but on diffusing technological benefits throughout society through careful national planning. This model diverges significantly from Washington’s. This is China’s long game.

In the mid-2010s, before becoming one of Washington’s most influential China strategists, Rush Doshi was a doctoral researcher at Harvard University embarking on an unusually painstaking exercise. He sifted through three decades of Chinese-language speeches, policy documents, party communiqués and military writings in search of an answer to a simple question: Did China really have a coherent strategy for challenging American primacy? Rather than a sudden turn under Chinese President Xi Jinping, Doshi found evidence of a remarkably consistent long-term effort to blunt, and eventually displace, U.S. dominance in the post-World War II international order.

“China is focusing not on frontier technological innovation, but on diffusing technological benefits throughout society through careful national planning.”

Under Xi’s leadership over the last decade and more, this long-term strategy has accelerated. The Belt and Road Initiative is its material infrastructural core, winding its way from ports in the Indian Ocean and rail corridors across Central Asia into Europe to fiber-optic cables reaching down through Pakistan to East Africa, and to ambitions for transcontinental power transmission systems and digital infrastructures.

By building out these material footings, China is constructing infrastructures to carry the leading technological transformations that will shape this century, and perhaps beyond. Artificial intelligence and an alternative internet are enrolling states into China’s enlarging sociotechnical system across Eurasia and Africa. The types of domestic transformations, including the most intense period of urbanization in human history and a radical reinvention of the domestic economy, have changed the nature of Chinese cities and infrastructure, generating cutting-edge modern metropolises such as Shanghai, Shenzhen and Chongqing, and are now being transmitted to other countries with Chinese labor, expertise and capital.

And because cities reflect the dominant societies that create them, Chinese influence will spread outward, just as new forms of connectivity will place China at the core of a new material and economic order. In its recently unveiled 15th Five-Year Plan , Beijing doubled down on the industrial strategy of using state economic planning to drive investment in technology, infrastructure and dominance of critical supply chains that has underpinned its rise for four decades. Read Noema in print.

It is not enough for Silicon Valley to be the first to push the frontiers of new technologies. Being first will not alone lead to victory. The United States continues to be a world leader in many frontier technologies, including artificial intelligence, advanced semiconductors, cloud computing infrastructure, biotechnology platforms, space launch systems and quantum computing research. But the old free market model of cascading benefits from private enterprise and investment that then flow throughout the economy is now being pitted against a very different model: a huge state willing to carefully direct its vast resources to diffuse technology throughout its own society and, via the mechanisms of transnational infrastructure it is building beyond its own borders, to reshape international society.

Although the commanding heights of creativity and innovation may continue to reside in the U.S., China is building the infrastructures of diffusion that may ultimately extract the greatest benefit from those innovations, increasing its soft power, influence and appeal to other states along the way.

The big labs of Silicon Valley are currently gripped by fear that China’s approach to opening its AI models to international partners may undermine the closed-source, proprietary model approach developed by U.S. firms and give China growing global influence in the AI systems race. As Washington well knows, China has already developed significant control over many of the world’s critical supply chains needed for those technologies, including those for processed rare earths vital for building the digital architectures and artificial intelligences of the future, and for batteries and robotics.

As Sullivan has argued, it will be the societies that most successfully capture and deploy resources at scale that win the future, and many of those resources reside far from America’s shores. These are the “nodes of leverage,” as Sullivan describes them. Donald Trump found this out when trying to apply pressure through tariffs on China.

There are challenges to be sure. China has an aging population, a burgeoning debt cloud, an extended property sector crisis and still lacks genuine soft power and allies. Its increasingly centralized political system could yet become a source of weakness. And yet it has realized that successful grand strategy today requires thinking about space and time in ways that register the importance of both transnational scale and the long term. If the U.S. is to compete successfully, it will need to remember how to think in those terms.

In Search Of Time Future

How can the United States rework its political culture and institutions to take these concerns on board and shape its strategic orientation toward a new form of international society fit for the current century?

Although we have come to think that the unfettered free market and capitalism’s unimpeded creative energy led to the Soviet Union’s defeat, this reflects historical forgetfulness. During the Cold War, the federal government invested both at home and abroad to shape the outcome of that hegemonic contest.

“It is not enough for Silicon Valley to be the first to push the frontiers of new technologies. Being first will not alone lead to victory.”

Many constituents in the U.S. have forgotten the historical importance of what the Harvard historian Charles Maier called the “ Project-State ” – states driven by a deep sense of ideological and historical mission that use their resources to generate far-reaching social, political and economic transformation. Such states might be democratic or authoritarian in character and ideological mission. Maier writes of the history of Fascist Italy, Nazi Germany and Soviet Russia, but also of the United States under President Franklin Roosevelt’s New Deal, and the restructuring of both domestic and international society that Roosevelt’s project-state enacted.

The project-state, by its very nature, plays a long game. It cannot exist in the culture of short-termism and the diminished temporal horizon of contemporary America. Today, China, with its clear sense of ideological mission and long-term strategic planning, more closely resembles the history-making project-states of the past. Maier, now in his late 80s, has expressed concern that the U.S. — hollowed out by market ideology, rising populism and a loss of national cohesion and democratic mission — has forgotten its sense of itself as a collective, intergenerational history-shaping project.

Success for great powers needs long-term purpose: a shaping vision of how to build a better domestic and international society that can solve the pressing problems of the day without discounting the future. If it is to change direction, future American power would need to consider and build into its strategic planning all of the issues raised here: the relationship between state industrial policy and technological innovation, the way in which innovations are diffused through society, as well as the infrastructures and urban environments needed to shape lives through technological advance — not just domestically but transnationally.

Above all, democracies must transcend their culture of short-termism and treat rebuilding their domestic and shared international societies as a long-term intergenerational project. Rather than simply looking back on its 250th anniversary, the United States must play the long game and consider the next 250 years.

Sullivan’s instinct that the material well-being and economic prospects of the middle and working classes must be the starting point is a good one, as is the deliberate linking of international and domestic society. But more needs to be done to fully conceptualize and forge a new link between them.

Many paths might be taken, but some more interesting and influential debates are underway that could shape a post-Trump and post-MAGA direction. The so-called abundance agenda, for all the attention and subsequent criticism it received, provides a helpful template for moving beyond the now-exhausted laissez-faire of the last half-century.

Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson argue for accelerating the latent yet blocked productive potential of American technology and society. They seek to rediscover the lost optimism and long-termism that once defined America — a new socio-technical imaginary of the future — alongside the institutional and state capability needed to realize it.

America’s ability to construct a future better than its past, despite many of the technological building blocks already in place, is, they argue, strangled by red tape, an excessively legalistic culture, increasingly polarized politics, and most crucially, a loss of the state’s capacity to build, coordinate and direct long-term national development.

In many domains like clean energy, scientific and biomedical innovation, technological breakthroughs exist, but the infrastructures of diffusion are absent because of a lack of state-driven investment and fragmented governance. Transmission and grid infrastructure for solar, wind, geothermal and nuclear technologies are lagging. America is a leader in biomedical science, but greater state investment in scientific institutions could drive research into real-world applications and rollouts. America’s problem has never been the frontier, but the failure to deploy and diffuse technologies at scale in areas where markets alone have proven unable to coordinate collective action.

The abundance agenda is animated by the transformative potential of frontier technologies like artificial intelligence, clean energy, biotechnology and advanced manufacturing, but it requires technological innovation to be matched by the institutional ability to deploy it through renewed investment in infrastructure, scientific research, energy transmission and the transition to a sustainable energy system.

At its heart is a politics of building: restoring the state’s capacity not merely to regulate markets, but also to shape them in pursuit of long-term national renewal. One missing policy mechanism is a sovereign infrastructure institution, such as a Strategic Investment Fund , that could unlock private capital reluctant to take on the long-term investment risks required for major national and international infrastructure projects. In this way, vast pools of private capital may be unlocked that could help the United States and its allies match the infrastructure-building scale and strategic reach of China’s Belt and Road Initiative.

“America’s problem has never been the frontier, but the failure to deploy and diffuse technologies at scale in areas where markets alone have proven unable to coordinate collective action.”

When the United States constructed the post-World War II architecture, it inevitably brought many elements of its own domestic experience to that task. The ideological underpinnings of Roosevelt’s New Deal, with its focus on federal state-led programs of reform and renewal after the Great Depression, also shaped many of the financial and institutional governance structures of the new multilateral order — specifically the United Nations. This established a link between a great power state’s domestic agenda and its ability to craft a wider international order. The New Deal emerged out of the New York context, where Roosevelt cut his teeth politically before becoming president.

Today, however, technology is likely to be at the core of any renewal of the United States’ social contract, so we must look to California for clues about its development. The transformational impact on society of advances in artificial intelligence will test what type of political economy will shape America and its key allies’ futures.

California’s outgoing governor, Gavin Newsom, who’s also potentially gearing up for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028, has had a ringside seat as Silicon Valley has pushed the boundaries of AI in recent years. Newsom has watched this development and tried to think about the way progressives can harness it to improve society. Rather than accepting the current paradigm, his progressive backers have been drawn to the idea of an “ AI New Deal ,” echoing an earlier time of similar economic instability and rising authoritarian powers. He has also referenced the abundance agenda in state legislation and argued for an “abundant mindset.”

Newsom has expressed concern for the disruptive and potentially harmful effects of AI for American workers, issuing executive orders directing state agencies, academia and industry to think about safety nets for displaced workers, including state subsidies incentivizing companies to retain and upskill employees, as well as exploring the idea of “ universal basic capital ” providing workers with a stake in asset funds to offset wage losses brought about by AI. Newsom seems aware of the need for a social compact to absorb short-term shocks from the technology.

If Newsom were to gain the Democratic nomination in 2028, then his dispositions may well be an indication of America’s future direction — a subnational model transposed to the larger scale canvas of national and international politics, as well as a new direction in that perennial question of how to link the domestic to the international scale, and thus to the shaping of international order.

Although many pathways may be taken in the post-Trump, post-MAGA world, the ideas being pursued by thinkers, policymakers and politicians such as Newsom, Sullivan, and Klein and Thompson all point to the need to link American domestic renewal with international order. Sullivan’s foreign policy for the middle classes sought to learn from Trump’s appeal to working-class Americans.

But where Trump’s instinctively treats America’s relationship with the rest of the world and its allies as a zero-sum game, Sullivan recognizes that the relationship must be bidirectional and therefore — mutually beneficial. U.S. foreign policy must return to a form of moral leadership. Trump’s approach breaks the symbiotic connection between a beneficial international order and the public goods and advantages that flow from it. Critically, it also threatens to deny the United States the transnational scale and reach to compete effectively with China if its allies turn away.

Here then is a coda, from, of all places, Angola. In December 2024, Biden became the first American president in nearly a decade to visit a sub-Saharan African country. For it was in Angola that one of the flagship transnational infrastructure projects of the U.S.-led G7 Partnership for Global Infrastructure Investment (PGII) was to begin — the Lobito Trans-Africa Corridor project — a strategic transport and logistics corridor to connect the port city of Lobito by railway to the interior of the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia, areas rich in critical minerals like cobalt, copper and other rare earths for the technological transitions in both clean energy and AI. Angola symbolized a shift in American foreign policy toward long-term investment in transnational infrastructure, driven by a dawning realization of China’s growing influence.

“U.S. foreign policy must return to a form of moral leadership.”

With the Trans-Africa Corridor project and the even more ambitious India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor project under the Biden administration, the U.S. and its allies had started to copy some of China’s playbook: a focus on maritime ports, transport connectivity through corridor development, securing supply chains of critical minerals, and support for digital infrastructure. The big difference was the central role of private-sector finance, rather than direct state investment as in the Chinese model.

Transnational infrastructure as geopolitics had belatedly made its way to the core of U.S. foreign policy; an overdue turn to thinking about the nature of strategic competition on both spatial and temporal scales. With the change in administration, America moved away from this approach.

The Twilight Of Primacy?

Paths to renewal and decline are both on offer. If the wrong path is taken, then the moment of American primacy will have lasted about a century — a familiar historical pattern.

A more exceptional path would be for a Great Power to reforge that link between a compelling renewed domestic social, political and economic model, and a different form of international order that crafts a new future for the United States and others. At the same time, China is also feeling its way toward its own version of such a link. And, as Xi has made clear time and again, China feels that time is on its side.

Great powers are ultimately judged not by the wealth they accumulate or the weapons they possess, but by the futures they can persuade others to inhabit. All of the major challenges that face humanity — the development of artificial intelligence, the transition to clean and sustainable energy, the working out of a new model for the world economy, the relationship of people to their political institutions, the balance of power between ambitious and competitive states — are subsumed by this overarching task of linking a successful domestic paradigm to the architecture of international order.

Can the next generation of U.S. leadership rise to these challenges as their forebears once did? The central question facing this generation of policymakers is whose future they want Americans to live in: the one they build, or somebody else’s.

stories.body:
Commissioner Stéphane Séjourné says bloc will support 46 strategic projects including lithium and rare earths plants

The EU is “pulling out all the stops” to fend off an imminent potential trade crisis with China , the industry commissioner, Stéphane Séjourné, has said, as the bloc announced its backing for a string of critical materials projects.

Séjourné said on Friday that the EU would support 46 new strategic projects to accelerate supplies of critical raw materials by 2030 across the bloc.

“We could face a crisis in the coming months,” he said. “We may face trade tensions that could also trigger a crisis in a number of sectors. We need to be prepared for that. And we’re getting ready right now.”

The new projects include plants for supplies of lithium, gallium and rare earths needed for the auto, defence and renewable energy industries, with a funding cost of €21bn (£17.8bn).

They were unveiled just as the EU works to avert a trade war with China , with the trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, continuing talks on Friday in Beijing aimed at reducing China’s “unsustainable” £1bn-a-day trade surplus with the bloc.

“We’re pulling out all the stops to move as quickly as possible. The primary objective is the targets set by law, and beyond that, there’s a geopolitical challenge that could catch up with us very quickly,” said Séjourné.

“Mines are opening, factories are being built, financing agreements are being signed, and a European value chain is emerging,” Séjourné added.

Amid some scepticism over the EU’s ability to meet its 2030 targets to reduce dependencies on China, Séjourné cited three “emblematic” projects which have previously been identified as strategic, earmarking them for accelerated permits.

These included a rare earths plant near Pau in south-western France. The Carester plant, which is expected to be up and running in late 2026, produces dysprosium and terbium, “two raw materials for which we are almost entirely dependent on China”, used in magnets for electric vehicles and offshore wind turbines.

“This single project could account for about 15% of global production of these oxides. That is no small feat,” Séjourné said.

He also name-checked a gallium plant in Greece which is already up and running.

The third, Keliber, a lithium extraction and processing plant in Finland, is also operational after €150m support from the European Investment Bank.

The 46 projects are the second batch of initiatives to receive flagship status since the Critical Raw Materials Act of 2024, which legally mandates the European Commission to reduce the bloc’s dependency on foreign countries.

after newsletter promotion

The EU hopes to follow in the footsteps of Japan, which has reduced dependency on China for rare earths to 60% from 90% since 2011, when Beijing prohibited exports of about 20 entities to Japan, claiming they were being used for military purposes.

Although the flagship status does not bring the projects direct funds, it enables accelerated permitting, and help in mobilising funds.

However, there has been criticism in industry within the EU that the scheme is not strong enough to deliver targets to mine 10%, process 40% and recycle 25% of the bloc’s needs by 2030.

The French lithium refiner Viridian Lithium, which received EU strategic status in 2025, went into judicial liquidation in March this year.

Earlier this year, a group of 23 of the 60 projects designated strategic in 2025 wrote to the European Commission calling for more action to “urgently unlock projects, particularly those working towards final investment decision which face acute liquidity and market pressure and ​immediate jeopardy”.

Séjourné said member states had unlocked €1bn for six of the projects, with the European Investment Bank providing another €660m for eight projects.

stories.body:
Whether on the frontline in Ukraine or skate parks in Soweto, the genre is still a vital outlet for disaffected people everywhere. Here, musicians explain how they rage against the machine

Ukraine: ‘I was lucky not to die. I had guitars with me on the frontline’

Andriy Zholob , vocalist/guitarist , Beton : When MTV arrived in Ukraine , I heard Nirvana, the Offspring, Bad Brains, Social Distortion and thrash metal, and realised that all this started from punk rock. Our drummer and I were in a ska-punk band first, but when our vocalist became pregnant we started Beton in 2017 and played lots of festivals.

Everything changed with the invasion. In 2022, I started military service as a surgeon on the frontline. We were attacked many times and on at least four occasions I was lucky not to die. I had guitars with me on the frontline and every evening we’d play just to relax. At one point, my commander gave me eight days off to record a battle song for our brigade and Beton did a cover of the Clash’s London Calling – Kyiv Calling – to raise money for the Ukrainian resistance. I wanted to use punk rock to stand against evil.

I finished my service two years ago, quit medicine and now work with veterans, many of whom come to our gigs. There are guys and girls with prosthetics, slam dancing, singing along and everything. It’s a real moment of punk rock unity. We play two or three shows every month, but I like to spend time in the mountains. Although I play punk rock, sometimes I need silence.

Morocco and Spain: ‘People would tell me: you love Satan’

Nao, vocalist, Taqbir : In the Muslim community of Morocco , where I come from, the punk look is not accepted. For a long time, I had to perform anonymously, with my face covered, in case people recognised me and wanted to hurt me. Being a punk is not for the faint-hearted. Even in Spain, where I live now, I felt isolated as an immigrant and as a woman who did crazy things to my hair. People would tell me: “You love Satan.”

I heard Crass when I was 13. They were the first band I heard where I recognised myself in the lyrics, because I felt oppressed by religion. Then through chatting with friends online, I discovered more. I’d go to shows in Madrid, take off my hijab and wear makeup. It was a double life that meant I finally felt free to be myself, but for a long time punk cost me my relationship with my family.

Being in Taqbir really helped. I was very angry, so fronting the band was like a cure for this rage. People seem to connect with the rawness. We’ve played in north Africa and the UK and my dream is to be able one day to play in Morocco. Punk has helped me see that things don’t have to be black and white: people can be punk and Muslim and gay. Although there’s anger, our message is positive. If you’re feeling oppressed or that you cannot be yourself in this society, Taqbir are for you.

South Africa: ‘Being from Soweto automatically makes you political’

Abdula Skink, vocalist, Twenty One Children : A lot of kids in Johannesburg got into punk because there were no jobs or infrastructure for us. I grew up in a hip-hop house, but found bands such as Suicidal Tendencies and Black Flag through video games and older friends who skated. Punk just flicked all these switches in my head. Our guitarist, Thula, used to play in TCIYF, the first all-black punk band in South Africa . When we started our band in 2023, I was an assistant teacher for 21 autistic kids, so that became our name. I was also 21, so it felt like a lucky number.

Being from Soweto automatically makes you political. All the great revolutionaries – Hugh Masekela, Nobel prize winners, Desmond Tutu and so on – came from here. Our motto is: if something isn’t true, we won’t sing about it. Our song Scab is about a time I was stopped by police because I was skating through a historically Afrikaans/white area. I had green hair and the policeman was like: “You’re on drugs.” He ripped my Suicidal Tendencies T-shirt, dropped my laptop from my bag on the street and tried to take my skateboard. I wasn’t doing anything illegal. They were just fucking with me. Mostly, we try to make a difference in our communities. Thula built the first DIY skate park in Soweto; we’ve done charity shows for orphanages and such. For us, punk is not so much a livelihood but a way of life.

India: ‘We were bombarded with threatening messages’

Aditya Naik, vocalist/guitarist, Punk on Toast : I grew up listening to Bad Religion, NOFX, the Sex Pistols and the Clash and saw a satirical commentary about our times, so I started the band when I was 17 so I could talk about what was happening around us. In India , you see cruelty or injustice on every corner, so we don’t relate to mainstream music, which ignores this.

At the moment, there’s a lot of oppression of artists. After our song Modified talked about what the right wing are trying to do with us, we were bombarded with threatening messages online. People went through all our profiles, trying to find our phone numbers, where we live, our employers. It felt like being molested. Although we’ve had coverage in Rolling Stone India, the punk scene mostly flies under the radar, but that means we’re freer to sing about what we want.

We took part in the recent Cockroach protests in Mumbai , which alerted people to how things are and got everybody out on the street. Before that, India felt like a small elite club where everyone else is the “cockroaches”, so it was like seeing a phoenix: hope. The punk scene is growing, with our friends Pacifist and Emergency Trigger and bands such as the Light Years Explode and the Riot Peddlers. It’s more about documenting our times and standing for what’s right rather than selling lots of records, but punk rock gave me the greatest superpower: question everything.

Brazil: ‘Under a military dictatorship, there were kids brave enough to play with passion and fury’

Henrike Baliu , vocalist, Blind Pigs and Armada : When the original UK punk explosion happened in 1977, my dad was a naval engineer stationed in Southampton. He saw the Boomtown Rats performing Lookin’ After No 1 on Top of the Pops and told the guy in the record shop: “Give me everything you’ve got” – which meant the Sex Pistols, Generation X and so on.

Years later, when I was 12, I played some of my dad’s records to my friends and they told me about the punk scene in Brazil . Bands such as Ratos de Porão, Inocentes and Cólera sang about life under a military dictatorship, which Brazil was in the 80s. People were disappearing or being murdered, so it blows my mind that under a dictatorship with virtually zero news, poverty and police brutality there were kids with spiky hair brave enough to wear fake leather jackets and play with passion and fury. Those bands were pioneers who paved the way for us.

Blind Pigs were probably the biggest punk band in Brazil over the last 30 years, but now I’m focused on Armada. We are bilingual and sing in Portuguese and English. When we recorded our English language album, Tales of Treason, the country was going through another crazy time politically and the right wing were on the rise again. With the music, I wanted to warn people to learn from history: “Dudes, you don’t want that again.”

Latvia: ‘On stage I let out all my anger’

Evisa Petrovska, vocalist, Depustūtes : In high school, I didn’t really like pop, so I got into metal, but I felt it was missing lyrical depth, so punk really resonated. Ramones and the Sex Pistols sang about the same stuff that made me mad or frustrated. The Dead Kennedys’ political commentary really connected and then I discovered riot grrrl. As I got older, I realised there was a punk scene here in Riga and a whole community of people like me.

There’s so much going on in the world – I’ll never run out of topics and writing and singing in the band never gets boring. On stage, I let out all my anger. Whether I’m running or crawling on the floor, it’s just pure emotion. Singing in Latvian makes it easier to sing about local politics. Lately, we’ve been addressing how people who actually benefit society aren’t getting paid as well as those who aren’t, but I sing about societal norms and stereotyping.

Our song Mrs Pieklājība (Mrs Polite) starts, in a mocking way: “I love listening to men and being obedient.” It was inspired by people telling me “you should smile more” or “women don’t dress like that”. There’s always been at least two women in the band, but most people are really supportive. I love inspiring other girls’ lives. A lot of them come up after shows and say: “That was so inspiring. I wish I could speak as freely as you.”

China: ‘Our albums were confiscated and our work was taken offline’

Wu Wei, vocalist, SMZB : Wuhan and Beijing were the first cities in China to have punk music. I founded the first punk band in Wuhan in 1996 after falling in love with tapes that my friends sent me from the US – initially the Sex Pistols, the Clash, Ramones and then bands with other styles, such as US Bombs, Suicide Machine and Rancid. Through punk, I finally found a way to express myself. Although the scene is still quite small, we were one of the first bands to go on national tours, which influenced the development of punk in other cities. We sing about the environment we operate in: political aspects and things I’ve witnessed in daily life under the system in China.

A few years ago, the authorities prohibited us from performing. Some albums were confiscated, our work was taken offline and our record company was forced to terminate our contract. Despite this, our audiences have a wide age span and range from other punks and bands to art workers, students and ordinary wage-earners. Punk has brought me so many things, from running the bar Wuhan Prison to my personal life. I’ve now settled in the UK with my family, but frequently return to Wuhan for rehearsals and recording. SMZB just released a bilingual album, When the Party Is Over, for our 30th anniversary. Punk has given me my life.

Greenland: ‘I’m 38, a father, still have my piercings and still consider myself a punk’

Jenseeraq Olsen, vocalist/guitarist, Uummat : We have a running joke with Iceland that they are green and we are ice, so most people live on the coast. I was in Denmark for a festival recently and realised that there were more people there – 70,000 – than the entire Greenlandic population. Punk is very much a minority interest here, but I was always rebellious when I was young and didn’t like the mainstream pop my friends were into.

After I saw an advert for Blink-182’s Enema of the State album after the movie American Pie, I realised they were the band I’d been searching for. I was teased for having multicoloured hair and ripped clothes, but Blink were a big influence on Uummat, which means “heart”. We were different from other bands in Greenland and people connected with it: we’ve played to 2,000 people.

I’ve never really written political songs, but Trump’s threat to annex Greenland has made a lot of people emotional, stressed and nervous, which I’m sure will come out in the music. I’m 38, a father and manage a youth centre now, but Blink resonate as much as they did when I was 15. I still have my piercings and I still consider myself a punk. Meanwhile, my 11-year-old son listens to the same music and plays guitar like me. He thinks labels like “punk” are for adults, but he likes the word, so he’ll probably follow in my footsteps.

stories.title: Polanski vows to stay as Green leader as he faces criticism after by-election defeat
stories.summary: Jewish Greens' leader has said Polanski should resign in the wake of a Zionism row and by-election defeat.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:

Polanski was challenged on Radio 4's Today over whether he thinks Israel has a right to exist

Published 9 October 2026, 11:11 BST

Zack Polanski has vowed to stay on as Green Party leader after his by-election defeat, as he faced pressure from within his own party to resign.

The leader of the Jewish Greens, Vivien Lichtenstein, said on Friday he should resign, adding it was a "big mistake" for him to have dodged a debate about a party conference motion that declared Zionism a form of racism.

Lichtenstein's comments come after former Green Party leader Caroline Lucas accused Polanski of failing to show leadership over the Zionism row.

Polanski, who came second to Labour overnight in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, told BBC Breakfast he would "absolutely" stay on as leader and "of course" had not questioned that.

The Greens had hoped to take the seat, previously held by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, after a by-election success earlier this year .

Polanski lost out in Thursday's contest in London to Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali, who secured 45% of the vote to his 33% - but the Green vote share was up by 22% on the 2024 general election.

In her comments calling on Polanski to resign, Lichtenstein told Times Radio: "I don't know which Jewish members of the party he's been working with – it certainly hasn't been with the Jewish Greens committee."

Her criticisms were similar to those of former Green Party leader Caroline Lucas who said Polanski should have attended the vote on the conference motion on Sunday.

The motion, which was passed by rank-and-file members to become official party policy, defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

Lucas described the motion as "dangerous" and "flawed from top to bottom".

She later posted on X to clarify she was "not calling on Zack to step down" and she welcomed that Polanski had "indicated he shares some of my concerns on the Zionism motion".

"Now the party needs to come together to make the urgent changes needed to take us forward," she said.

'Racist ideology'

Polanski defended his absence from the controversial motion vote in Brighton, saying he was busy campaigning in the North London constituency.

Asked if he would resign, he said: "Of course I can carry on as leader of the Green Party."

He added: "Yes, I've taken a loss tonight but our movement is so much bigger than one election or one motion."

Having not answered questions about the Zionism vote for most of this week, Polanski confirmed in interviews on Friday that he would not have voted for the "imperfect" motion without it being amended.

However, he said "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by a racist ideology".

Several UN reports have accused the Israeli government of committing war crimes which amount to genocide in Gaza. Israel has repeatedly denied all such allegations.

On Friday morning, following the Zionism row, Polanski was asked repeatedly on BBC Radio 4's Today programme whether he believes Israel has a right to exist.

"I don't believe any state has the right to oppress or to commit apartheid and certainly not genocide on another people," he said, adding: "I don't believe that's a state that anyone should be supporting."

Asked by presenter Nick Robinson for a "yes/no" answer on this question, he said: "I've repeated many times that I want to see equal rights for Israelis and Palestinians - at the moment Palestinians don't have equal rights so I think I'm answering your question really clearly."

Anger on both sides

In private, plenty of longstanding Green figures remain frustrated and accuse Polanski of being "missing in action" over the motion.

They say the result is an untenable situation where he leads a party whose policy on the Middle East he disagrees with.

"He is in danger of losing the confidence of both wings," one critic pointed out, referring to how some supporters of the motion have now been left irritated too by Polanski's refusal to publicly back them.

Polanski faces greatest crisis of his leadership so far Published 8 hours ago

Labour sees off Green challenge to win Holborn by-election Published 4 hours ago

But given his popularity among the grassroots, he may be safe from a leadership challenge in the near future.

Jonathan Bartley, the Green co-leader from 2016 to 2021, called on Polanski to "put his hands up" and "say sorry" - but did not demand he quit.

"I think [the vote] was a failure of leadership from Zack and there is a certain toxicity now around the Green Party," he told BBC Radio 4's World at One.

Bartley said the Green brand "needs to be detoxified", adding the party had seen an influx in members that have "maybe come from the left of the Labour Party, maybe from [Jeremy Corbyn's] Your Party" but "we're losing some older voters".

The party's next scheduled leadership ballot takes place in summer 2027 - and Bartley said he thinks Polanski will face a challenger.

Sian Berry, Green MP for Brighton Pavilion, said on Friday she was ready to work with colleagues "to restore trust in our processes and our party, fix the serious flaws in the motion that was passed" and build more inclusive policies.

The Green leader has faced days of pressure over the Zionism motion. Four of the five Green MPs and one of the party's two deputy leaders opposed it, the Green deputy in Wales and some councillors resigned, while some local members and the European Green Party have distanced themselves from it.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called on Polanski to reverse the "completely wrong" motion.

Meanwhile, Labour chair Bridget Phillipson drew comparisons with her party's previous antisemitism scandal , telling the BBC she felt the Greens now face a "serious problem" with antisemitism.

Polanski has said anti-Zionism and antisemitism are distinct from each other and said nobody will be excluded from the party on the basis of their faith, place of worship or religious body.

stories.title: Burnham promises to curb non-compete rules in job contracts
stories.summary: The prime minister says restrictions on what workers can do after leaving roles have "gone too far".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 2 hours ago

Andy Burnham has promised to curb companies' ability to restrict what their workers can do after leaving their job.

In a speech, the prime minister said the use of non-compete clauses in employment contracts had "gone too far" and was holding innovative UK companies back.

He added the clauses had forced workers to go without pay after leaving a role, as well as making it harder for growing firms to hire new staff.

Ahead of the Budget later this month, he also said there was "more to do" on tax to encourage promising firms to stay in the UK.

Sir Keir Starmer's government had been exploring possible restrictions on non-compete clauses since late last year, including a total ban, banning them above a certain salary threshold, or limiting how long they can last.

Although commonly associated with the financial services and technology sectors, research cited by the government has estimated around 5 million jobs in Britain are covered by the clauses, typically lasting around six months.

Speaking at a business summit in Manchester, Burnham confirmed his government would press ahead with new legislation to ensure the clauses can "no longer be a barrier" to hiring new staff.

He added that their use had stopped workers leaving to join other companies, or founding their own firms instead, adding: "I think that's a drag on innovation."

Referencing a landmark 1995 court ruling that is credited with revolutionising the football transfer market in Europe, he said he hoped reining in non-compete clauses could prove the "Bosman ruling for the innovation sector".

Investor confidence concerns

Burnham did not specify the scope of the restrictions he is planning, but suggested they would apply to the "everyday economy" as well as helping "promising start-ups and scaling firms".

It is understood that the government is planning to unveil details of the proposed restrictions, which were first reported by Politico , external and The Financial Times , external , alongside the Budget on 28 October.

The previous Conservative government had ruled out a total ban , external on non-compete clauses, after hearing from employers that it could reduce investor confidence in the UK or prompt companies to tighten how they share information internally.

The prime minister sought to frame the announcement on non-compete clauses as part of a wider government pitch to boost innovative sectors of the economy.

He told the summit that although the UK was home to outstanding research and start-ups, too many companies had gone abroad in search of investment.

He also signalled that the government would "say more" at the Budget about plans to use public investment as a way to encourage private funding in the economy.

He added that he wanted all UK regions to have a dedicated fund to do this, modelled on the Good Growth Fund launched in Greater Manchester last year, during his tenure as mayor of the city-region.

He also hinted that the government was looking at the tax system to ensure the UK can retain high-growth companies.

He said: "One of our biggest challenges is breaking through our own ceiling. Too often, our best ideas are developed and scaled overseas, and with it the jobs, technology and investment that goes with them."

"So I know there is more to do to fix that, specifically on tax, to encourage people to stay and scale."

stories.title: Ex-first minister Mark Drakeford suggests Wales Office should go
stories.summary: Created 60 years ago, most of the powers it used to hold were transferred to Cardiff Bay in 1999.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Mark Drakeford was first minister from December 2018 to March 2024

Published 3 hours ago

Former Labour First Minister Mark Drakeford has said it is time to consider scrapping the UK government's Wales Office.

Drakeford said "the time has come" to think about abolishing the department, which was largely stripped of its powers when devolution began in 1999.

Asked on S4C's Y Byd yn ei Le if he would be happy to get rid of the Wales Office, Drakeford said: "Yes, I think the time has come for us to think about that."

But Labour MP Ruth Jones described the suggestion as "foolish", arguing Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock was "fighting the corner for Wales".

The future of the Wales Office has been the subject of regular speculation since devolution, with successive UK governments considering whether its functions could be folded into a single department, also covering Scotland and Northern Ireland.

Earlier this year, then-First Minister Eluned Morgan said there remained " a role " for the Welsh secretary, but argued the post should be "the voice of Wales at the cabinet table" rather than "the UK government's voice in Wales".

Under a previous UK Labour government, Peter Hain combined cabinet responsibility for Wales and Northern Ireland between 2005 and 2007.

Asked if he would be happy to get rid of the Wales Office, Drakeford said: "Yes, I think the time has come for us to think about that.

"Of course, [former Labour prime minister] Tony Blair thought of this too.

"This has been part of discussions in Westminster not only now but for more than a decade."

The post of Welsh secretary, or secretary of state for Wales, was created by Harold Wilson's Labour government in October 1964, with the Welsh Office opening the following April.

In 1999 the Welsh Office's powers over areas including health, education, environment, agriculture and transport were taken over by the Welsh Assembly, now known as the Senedd , and what remained of the UK government department was given the title of Wales Office.

Stephen Kinnock was appointed Welsh secretary by Andy Burnham in July

Interviewed on BBC Radio Wales Breakfast on Friday , Ruth Jones dismissed the idea of abolishing it.

"I've got tremendous respect for Mark Drakeford but, let's be honest, he's now retired and, therefore, let the politicians who are elected to get on with the job get on with the job," she said.

"In terms of the Wales Office, the only person from Wales actually at the [UK] cabinet table is the secretary of state for Wales, and he is there fighting the corner for Wales.

"So I would say to disband that would be foolish."
